speechtext: Bill (No. 118) for the relief of James Brown considered in committee and reported.
CLARKE (West Toronto) moved the third reading of the Bill.

Before this Bill is read the third time, Mr. Speaker, I desire, for more than the third time, to renew my protest against the method pursued by this parliament with regard to the granting of divorces. The system is one which, I believe, cannot be justified upon any principle of law or good sense. If a divorce is to be granted at all, it is, of course, to be granted for reasons- for reasons which the law will define. I do not believe that the parliament of Can-ana is the body that can properly deal with these reasons and render a decision upon them. The case before this House is one that I know nothing about; it is one that, I venture to say, not one member of this
House in ten has taken the trouble to examine. We are called upon to pass judgment in a case of the very greatest importance to the parties interested, and we do this, Sir, in a way that is nothing less than a travesty upon justice. If divorces are to be granted in this country, they should be granted by a properly constituted court, a court which shall take evidence and examine into the facts bearing upon the case, a court that shall render its judgment in accordance with the evidence. I repeat that, however it may be in the other branch of the Dominion legislature-where these cases may receive the consideration which they should receive-this case and cases of this character have not received and do not receive that degree of consideration here. The evidence is not published, The investigation is a sort of Star Chamber investigation; and I protest again, as I have often protested, that, if we are to grant divorces in Canada at all, if we are to recognize any cause as sufficient for granting a divorce, it is time that these matters should be placed in the hands of a proper legal tribunal.

ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) When the representatives from Nova Scotia first came to Ottawa after confederation, among the things that they found in existence were dual representation and the holding of elections in different parts of the country at times selected by the government. We had that changed. By the influence and example, I think, of the representatives from Nova Scotia, we had dual representation abolished and simultaneous polling adopted. But we found also a system of granting divorces which has continued to this day. a system which, in my opinion is a perfect disgrace to our legislation and practice. In Nova Scotia, divorce cases are referred to a judge of the Supreme Court. Each case is decided in a day, and not an item of the evidence in either side is published in the newspapers. But here a lot of low, nasty literature finds its way to the public. I remember one case which arose in a former parliament of which I was a member. A man from Hamilton sought a divorce and his Bill was passed in the Senate. The Bill came before this House in due course. But the wife was a relative of a member of this House, and this member commanded such influence with the vote of the people who are opposed to divorce altogether and others that the Bill was defeated in this House. The petitioner had to come back to parliament a second year, and this he did. I remember his name perfectly, but I do not care about mentioning it. Before the Bill , was presented a second time the man whose influence had secured its defeat died. On the second application, the Bill was passed. This is all very well where a man has enough money to bear the heavy expense of securing such legislation. But a poor man or a poor woman, as the ease may be, must

be subject to all the trouble attending an application, and yet never be able to get a divorce. People have often referred to the small number of divorces granted in Canada, but that is owing to the fact that a poor man or a poor woman cannot obtain one under the present system. I think there is perhaps nothing in the annals of our legislation in the Senate or the House of Commons that requires amending as much as the present system of granting divorce.
Motion agreed to ; Bill read the third time, and passed. ,

seemed to be a difference of opinion in the committee. The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 155) to amend the Railway Act. He said : Notice of this Bill appears on the order paper, but at the moment when the orders were called, I did not have the draft of the Bill in my hand. This Bill is introduced for the purpose of making a small amendment to the general Railway Act to relieve certain sections or clauses of some ambiguity that seems to have arisen in respect to them. Under the law, as it stands at present, it has been recently interpreted by the courts that the powers of expropriation for the purpose of running a spur line from an existing railway to a gravel pit cannot be exercised, if, perchance, there should be a river or lake, or anything of that kind, intervening between the point at which they can carry the railway nearest to the gravel pit and to the gravel pit itself. It has been differently understood and it was not until recent questions had arisen that the point was brought to the attention of the department.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

House went into committee on the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to provide that in addition to the sums now remaining unborrowed and negotiable of the loans authorised by parliament by any Act heretofore passed, the Governor in Council be authorised to raise by way of loan :-
(a.) Such sum or sums of money, slot to exceed in the whole, the sum of fifteen million dollars, as may be required for the purpose of paying the floating indebtedness of Canada, and of meeting any expenditure authorized by the parliament of Canada ;-and
(b.) Such sum or sums of money as may be required from time to time, over and above any available sinking funds, to pay and discharge the Funded Debt of Canada, or any portion thereof, as the sjyne matures and becomes payable either in England or in Canada ;	[DOT]
Such sums to be raised in accordance with and under the provisions of that portion of chapter 29 of the Revised Statutes of Canada relating to the public debt and the raising of loans authorized by parliament, and the sums so raised to form part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada ; the rate of interest to be paid on any such loans not to exceed three and one-half per cent per annum.-The Min^ ister of Finance.

This is the resolution respecting the raising of money by way of loan, which the House will remember I announced in the budget speech. Our last loan Bill was passed in the year 1897, and was for $15,000,000, which is the smallest amount that has been taken for many years in a loan BUI. The outstanding borrowing powers at that date, including the $15,000,000, amounted to about $23,500,000. Out of that, we raised a loan of something less than $10,000,000 (two million pounds sterling) in 1897. We have a current floating indebtedness, as stated to the House, of about $6,000,000, and our savings bank 'borrowings, which are regarded in the light of a loan, have increased to 'the extent of about nine and a half million dollars. The net result of these and some other operations is, that our borrowing powers unused are now reduced to a very small figure, being on the 30th day of April, about $2,329,000. It is of course necessary that there should be a borrowing power available to the government from time to time. We have had no loan Bill since 1897, and we have been engaged in very large operations. I do not anticipate that it will be necessary
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: to go into the market for a loan during the current calendar year. The conditions of the money market are not too favourable, and they are likely to be better after the close of the war. However, that is a question which would be determined entirely by the state of the money market; as to- whether or not we shall continue to float temporary loans, or whether we shall place a public loan on the market. There is another clause in the Bill which gives us power to renew loans falling due. In that case there is no new obligation, but merely the power to renew such portions of these loans as may be necessary, after taking account of the available sinking funds.
What amount of loans are failing due, and at what interest ?
They are all set forth year by year in the public accounts, and a statement of those falling due within the next few years was made in the budget speech.
Very well.
I did not gather in what way the borrowing power under the Act of 1897 has been nearly all exhausted.
When you borrow money from the savings banks, have you to get authority under a loan Act ?

I think probably without a special Loan Act we could do it; but in stating to ithe House from time to time, the amount of our borrowings we have always included the savings bank deposits. We look upon the amount so taken as a public loan, and it is referred to in the Audit Act as one of the methods by which we may raise money.
Where was the temporary loan of $6,000,000 raised ?
The Bank of Montreal.
At what rate ?
3-J per cent, and I think there was a small portion of it which bore a shade above that.
At whait ralte of interest was the last loan ?
When you effect a temporary loan of that character for what period does it usually run ? In the present case i,s it for a definite period, or is it on demand, or is it renewable ?

It is sometimes for a fixed period of a year, but in the recent case it was only for six months. Owing to the state of the money market the banks preferred a short period of six months, and .they gave a better rate than for a year. That, of course, was advantageous to us, because it is renewable and the conditions may be better later.
How is the interest payable on these temporary loans ?
We have an annual appropriation which covers general interest as well as the specified bonds.
How frequently is interest paid ?
It is practically a discount; you discount Treasury Bills.

It is practically paid in advance.
Resolution reported ; read the second time, and agreed to.

Bill (No. 136) to amend the Fruit Marks Act, 1901 (the Minister of Agriculture) read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
change in the law is effected, and for what reason this amendment is introduced.

There is practically no change in the intention of the law. There was some confusion found in the enforcement of the Act as to the definition of the term ' packer,' a doubt arising as to whether it referred to the person on whose behalf the fruit was packed or the individual labourer who packed the fruit. The change makes It clear that It is the person on whose behalf the fruit is packed who is responsible fo;- the packing. Then, it has been found in practice that the trade wisli to adopt a standard of marks, and in this Bill we provide for marks of two different kinds-one set being XXX, XX and X ; the other being No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3. The reason the alternative is given is that in the maritime provinces the X marks are used, while in Ontario the numbers are used. People may use, along with these, their own private marks if they choose. We wish gradually to Introduce these marks, but we do not wish at present to make them absolutely the onlj marks.
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext: So far as the first change Is concerned, there seems to be every reason for it; but the other seems to be remarkably indefinite. What would von regard as a designation inconsistent with XXX ?

It would be one of an inferior grade ; for instance, No. 2 with XXX. The point more particularly is that a designation must not bo used inconsistent with X or XX. For instance, if ' specially selected ' were used with XX, it would be inconsistent; or if No. 1 were used with X, the two would be inconsistent. The difficulty arises in the fact that certain dealers have their own special grades, and if they were to use XX as the proper designation of the fruit, and were to accompany it with another designation of their own, which meant 1 special excellence ' or * highest grade,' that would be inconsistent with XX ; and though they might truthfully say that the fruit was legally marked, yet the marking would mislead the purchaser.
Have these changes been made at the suggestion of the fruit packers or fruit exporters ?

No, largely on the recommendation of fruit inspectors, who are charged with the enrol cement of the Act, and after discussion with the fruit dealers, and as a result of the experience of the last season.

Perhaps the min- Mr. CLARKE. Was any intimation given ister would be good enough to explain what to the fruit exporters as to the amendments 130



which were likely to be made in the Act of last session ?
They were discussed with them by the inspectors and when the inspectors were here about two weeks ago, they made these recommendations to me.
They discussed them previously with the fruit exporters ?
Yes.

I must say that this section strikes me as very indefinite

indeed, so indefinite as to be practically useless. If a dealer puts any other designation whatever upon a package of fruit, it must mean either the same thing as one of the marks already there, or it must modify it in some way. If it modifies it in any way is it to be regarded as inconsistent with it ?
It must mean practically the same thing.
If it means the same thing, what is the use of putting it on 1
Because certain dealers have marks which are known to their customers, and we do not wish to debar them from using those marks if they wish.

I cannot understand how ' specially selected ' can be inconsistent with XX or X, because that particular variety or class of fruit might be specially selected. The third-class might be specially selected as well as the first-class.
It would not be so considered by the trade.

But in dealing with an act of parliament it would be so determined. I am taking the English language in its ordinary acceptation ; I do not know anything about the technicalities of the trade. However, I do not suppose there is anything in this that can do any harm, though I fail to see that it can do any good. In fact, my hon. friend admitted last session that the chief merit of the Bill was that it could not do any harm. None of us were able to see how it could do any good.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE It has been found to do a great deal of good already.
Subsection 'a' requires that the packer shall mark the package with the initials of ' his ' Christian name. In the event of the exporter being a woman, how would the marks be designated ?
I believe that ' his ' is supposed to include ' her '.
Under what authority ? Is there an interpretation Act which makes ' his ' stand for ' her ' ?
I believe there is.

I regret very much that a Bill of this importance has been left to be dealt with by a thin House at the close of the session, when men who thoroughly understand the marking of fruit are absent.
I think it a great pity that this Bill has not been dealt with two months ago.

I would like to ask the minister if he has considered the question of making any description of No. 2 and No. 3 grades. I have had several communications from fruit growers who think that would be desirable, if possible.
The inspectors thought it was hardly feasible at the present time to make a correct and reliable definition of those grades.

Is it designated anywhere, either in this amendment or in the original Act, what XXX means ? If it is, this Act is of some service. If it is not, it is meaningless, and a man might put XXX on anything.

In section 6 of the original Act the definition of the first quality is given.
On section 2,
What is this change ?

It is simply to put in section 6 of the Act the words ' No. 1 ' as well as ' finest,' ' best ' and ' first quality.'
On section 3,

There are two ways in which this Act works. One is that the fruit shall be marked certain grades, and if the inspector finds it is not up to the grade he is authorized to put on the words 1 falsely marked.' There is another part of the Act which provides that the fruit shall be equal, all through the package, to its face, and there is no means of authorizing the inspector to label the package ' falsely packed ' where that provision of the Act is violated. I therefore ask to be given the authority to have the package labelled ' falsely packed ' as well as ' falsely marked.'
I sent copies of the Bill to several fruit exporters in Toronto, but have

only had a reply from one of them, so that I take it there cannot be any serious objection to the measure on the part of the others. The gentleman who did write me suggests that the words ' offered for sale ' should be added after the word 1 package ' in the first line of section f! and also in subsection 3, He gives as his reasons :
Owing to unavoidable hurry at times in getting fruit under cover, also deterioration1 when held any length of time, a shipper should not be held responsible for marks excepting when offering the fruit for sale ; were it otherwise every one handling same would become liable over and over again during a season ; I would therefore urge you to secure the insertion of the saving clause proposed ' offered for sale.'
It would be a harsh provision to have the Act amended as proposed in this Bill, and my correspondent suggests the advisability of adding the words 'offered for sale' so that a penalty will not he imposed upon the person whose name or initials are to be found on the outside of the barrel, unless the fruit contained in the barrel is being offered for sale.

I think the addition of those words would make the Act practically unworkable. When fruit is hurriedly put into a warehouse, the seller need not mark the package at all. It is only when the fruit is offered for sale, that the package need be marked. If the merchant is going to repack the fruit, he does not need to mark It until it is repacked. In the second place, the fruit is very frequently already sold and in the hands of a purchaser, and legal technicalities might interfere materially with the working of the Act, if these words were inserted. In the third place, we have often to deal with fruit in transit for the foreigu market, and I do not know how we could deal with it if these words were inserted. The fruit is in Toronto, and whether it is being offered for sale or has been sold or to whom it belongs, are questions which would raise a number of legal technicalities and obstruct the working of the Act. I think the danger which my hon. friend's correspondent fears is not a grave one, because he is not required to mark these packages at all until he is ready to offer them for sale.
If this Act be found to work harshly, I suppose the hon. gentleman would consent to an amendment at some future time ?
We have been enforcing the Act in a very lenient way up to the present and do not propose to administer it harshly at all.
What is the meaning of the third clause ?

It is the same as in the original Act, the only 1301
difference being that the inspector must give notice when he marks the packages ' falsely packed,' as he does in the case when he labels them ' falsely marked.' The object is to let the shipper or seller know that his fruit has been found to be wrongly marked, so that he take what steps he think necessary to protect himself. That is necessary when the fruit is in transit.
Are we to understand that if the inspector finds certain packages falsely marked, he will condemn the whole shipment, or only the barrel so marked.

That is a matter of regulation. I think I will have to make a regulation by which a certain number of barrels will be examined, and if found falsely marked or packed, the whole of that particular shipment will have to be thrown out. Last year we only marked the barrels examined, and serious complaint were made from the old country. In one case a lawsuit resulted over a large shipment, in which some barrels were marked and others were not, because not opened. I will have to make regulations to deal with this matter more strictly than in the past.

Frequently the shipper or his agent buys the orchard. Sometimes he has the picking done himself or he may pay so much for the whole orchard and repack the fruit after delivery. Supposing a lot of barrels were marked by the apple grower as instructed by the shipper and were not up to the standard of the inspection, and the purchaser intended having them repacked before being put on the market, how would the Act work then ?

Tn
such a case the barrels need not be marked at all. If they were inspected and the markers found them incorrect and fraudulent, I think that the person on whose behalf the apples were packed would be responsible and not the owner of the orchard.
I do not think that the hon. gentleman could, under this Act, make such a regulation as he speaks of. He could only have such fruit marked as not being up to the standard, which was really examined.
I think that is probably correct.

The regulation I propose would be that when a certain number of barrels are found wrongly packed or marked, the inspector would have to go through the whole lot. I do not propose that he should mark any package without examining it.
If out of a dozen barrels we found two falsely packed, would the inspector examine every barrel of the shipment ?

In the case of two out of ten, I would not consider it necessary for the inspector to go through the whole lot. But if he found seven or eight out of ten wrongly marked or packed, he would be instructed to examine every package.
If the inspector went through the whole lot, would the shipper not have the privilege of repacking ?
Certainly.

Where does the responsibility end in this matter? Suppose a retailer buys 50 or 100 barrels wrongly marked and offers them for sale. If the customer finds that the apples are not as represented, has he any recourse against the retailer ?
Yes.
Is that not likely to do injustice to the retailer ?
The intention of the Act was that the retailer should have his recourse against the person who sold the apples to him.

I think a case arose in Toronto where information was laid against the retailer. My recollection is not clear as to the circumstances, but I remember tnat it seemed to me at the time a very great injustice to the retailer that, after he had purchased so many barrels of apples and taken them into the store and sold certain barrels, one or more of which were found not to be as marked, proceedings should lie against the retailer. It is the person who packed the fruit and not the retailer who should be proceeded against.
The person who packs is responsible, but, by another section of the Act, anybody who offers for sale fruit improperly marked is also responsible.
Yet there is responsibility upon the retailer for every barrel, although he has had nothing to do with the packing.
Let him buy from a reputable party.

All the wholesale dealers are reputable parties. But does not the minister think it would be unjust to the retailer who buys twenty-five or fifty barrels of apples from a reputable firm and finds after they are sold by him, that some packages of the fruit are not as marked, that he should be proceeded against ? Would it not be better to provide that when a customer informs the department, the department should proceed against the wholesale man or shipper ?

I do not think it would do to debar the purchaser from proceeding against the retailer. But I may say that, under such circumstances as the hon. gentleman has indicated, the department would not proceed against the retailer, but against the parties who packed the fruit, or for whom it was packed. It would not do, however, to relieve the retailer of all responsibility.
Is there any provision under which the retailer has a remedy against the person who supplies him ?
The whole Act would give him that-he has the same remedy that the person who purchases from him has against him.
In what way ?
If he has purchased fruit, marked of a certain grade from A. B., a dealer or shipper or packer, he can proc'eed against that party if the fruit is not as marked.
For penalty ?

Yes, and for damages also.

At the Printing Bureau.
We have remedied that to a certain extent by the draperies the hon. gentleman has seen. The chief architect informs me he will be able to remedy it still further.

I would suggest that possibly another remedy might be found. The chairman's table and platform might be shifted to some point nearer the middle of the room at one side. It is almost impossible to hear anything now at the extreme end of the room.
Is the hon. gentleman quite sure about that ?
I am sure of that.

I would like to know how the total vote compares with that of the previous year. There are so many supplementaries, and the thing is in such a state of confusion, that we cannot exactly compare the expenditure of one year with that of another.

Last year we asked for $2,000 in the supplementary estimates, and this year for $3,000.
Parliament buildings, Ottawa

Addition to building over engine house and improvements in main vc-stibule, including elevators, &c., $21,500.'
What will that make the total cost ?
Does that cover the whole cost ?
Yes.

I would like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that his elevators are not very satisfactory. If there was a fire, all the members of the Railway Committee in that committee room would be burned up. If both elevators go wrong at once there would be no way of getting out.
I am sure the trouble is not with the elevators. Sometimes during the session the power has been short. During the recess I will see that that trouble is remedied.

Another trouble is the noise; the echo in that Railway Committee room is a very serious evil, and makes it almost impossible to do any business there. I suppose that will be attended to by the hon. minister in some way ?
I understand that in every new building there is something wrong with the acoustics.

I do not know where to place the seat of the chairman. For a time we put it just across where my hon. friend would like it to be; but on reflection we changed it. Of course, if the committee would like it to be changed, I have no objection.
Ottawa public buildings-heading, including salaries' of engineers, firemen, elevator attendants and caretaker, $12,000.
What is the cause of the increase ?

In the first place we have been obliged to buy 1,000 tons more coal on account of the greater number of public buildings we have in this city. Moreover, after public tenders last year, I was obliged to pay 65 cents per ton more for coal. I have just received tenders for next year, and the price of coal has still increased.
What kind of coal is it ?
Hard coal.
How do you buy it ?
By public tender.
How much does this increase the vote over the previous year?

By $12,000. We will be obliged to ask for more in the supplementary estimates. The total increase in the amount will be $24,000. We are obliged to pay $15,134 for an additional 1,000 tons of coal. We are obliged to pay the balance, because the price of coal has been increased.
Coal does not cost $15 a ton ?
No, we are paying $6.45 a ton.
And the increase on the total coal, together with the additional 1,000 tons, makes an increase of $15,000 altogether in the cost of coal for the buildings.
Quite so.
Has the hon. gentleman taken into consideration the question of making further provision for the public service in Ottawa by building'' instead of renting so many buildings about the city ?

We have considered the matter, but as the government have decided to erect a museum, a mint, and an astronomical observatory, my colleagues have thought that this year's budget is large enough, and we have not resolved to erect any new public buildings.
Mi'. BORDEN (Halifax). I am not urging the expenditure of any more money. I believe that possibly there might be a saving of money. The difficulty that has been mentioned in. the past is that you will have to buy land. I never could see the slightest necessity for buying more land. I believe that you have all the land required for putting up additional departmental buildings for the public service. As far as the observatory, the mint and buildings of that kind are concerned, I do not profess to know about them, but it seems to me that there is ample room for increasing the western public building, and there is ample room where the Supreme Court building is to erect another building. I think it would be well to consider whether or not that cannot be done, so as to save a considerable sum of money that is spent in rent, because, I believe the interest on the cost of these buildings would be less than the rent which the government are paying out in the city of Ottawa annually. ' Of course, I would not profess to speak about that with as much knowledge as that possessed by the hon. gentleman and the officers of his department. There is, however, no difficulty about the land.

The Supreme Court site has been pointed out to me several times and it is a very fine site indeed. I must admit that in my personal view it is better to erect the buildings required, but my hon. friend knows already, and he will perhaps know later on, that when budgets have reached a certain volume it is pretty difficult to get more money. We are paying out in the city of Ottawa $18,000 in rent. I am going to reduce that amount by $1,000 or $2,000, because I am going to improve the post office and provide accommodation there for the Department of Customs. We are now renting an office on Sparks street for that department. We are paying, as I was saying, about $1S,000 for rent, and, I suppose, $400,000. or $500,000, would erect a very flue building for the public service. I hope that next year we will be in a position to have a more definite policy upon that point.
Are not the office buildings which have been rented for the public service in this city under lease for ten years ? W'hat is the shortest lease ?

I think the shortest lease is one year. We are not bound by any length of time except in the case of the brick building at the corner of Metcalfe and Slater streets, where we are bound for ten years, of which two years have gone.
There are no other 'buildings leased for ten years 1
No.
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if he has any intention of building a new House of Commons chamber ?

Suggestions have been made that as the library is too small we might perhaps make an exchange, but this is a big question and at the present time I have not the information necessary to enable me to express an opinion upon it.

I suppose that those of us who are so favoured by our constituencies may expect to remain in this chamber for some years ? And if so, it seems to me that the hon. minister should direct his attention to the subject of the ventilation of the chamber. I shall not say very much about it, because I know it is a subject which has been discussed very often, but really, it seems to me an extraordinary thing that the House of Commons should be condemned to spend year after year in a chamber whose ventilation is absolutely disgraceful and prejudicial to the health, and that the matter should get so little attention. What is the reason that it is absolutely impossible to provide the House of Commons with pure air ? I think it is a most serious reflection upon the hon. Minister of Public Works, who has proved himself in every other direction so energetic and so capable. I hope that he will direct himself to the question of providing a remedy for what is unquestionably a scandalous evil.

I have, over and over again, called the attention of the chief architect to the ventilation of this House. Of course, we cannot change the nature of this chamber. It has been constructed on certain lines that we all know. It is a room in the middle of the building. As to the ventilation the chief architect tells me that he cannot see very well how he can change it now. It is as good as we can make it, although I grant it is not good.
It is not modern. It is an antiquated system.

If we open the windows over our heads there is a draught and everybody is sick.
I want parliament to be in good shape and in good health.
How long is the census building, at the corner of O'Connor and Sparks streets, leased for ?
Three years.
What portion of that time has expired ?
We have leased it for five years, but two years have gone, so that we are not bound for more than three years now.
Is it expected that the census will be completed in that time ?
It is not for me to answer that question.
I suppose you have an arrangement so that it can be renewed if necessary ?
We can always renew.
At that price ?
I have no desire to renew the lease of that building. I had enough trouble to put it through before.

Before leaving the matter referred to by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) of the ventilation of this chamber, I desire to say that during this session, we, on this side of the House, and more particularly those of us who sit on the middle row of seats, have found very great inconvenience and discomfort from the system of ventilating the chamber. I do not object to the air not being so pure at all times; we can put up with that, but there is another matter we do desire to enter our solemn protest against, and it is that .the fans that are used to force fresh air into the chamber are turned on while we are sitting in the chamber. When a cold blast of wind is driven directly against out-heads, being uncovered, no man is free from a severe cold. During the greater part of the session, 1 have been subject to a cold. I am sure this is a matter the minister can remedy by instructing the engineer that these fans shall not be turned on after six o'clock until the members have left the chamber.
Get out.

The Minister of Customs says ' get out,' but we are not provided with suitable and comfortable rooms in other parts of the building as he is.
We are compelled to remain here, and do our work and it is absolute cruelty to subject us to such treatment. I have spoken time and time about it, but without having any remedy applied. I think Mr. Chairman you will remember that when you sat on this side of the House you suffered in the same way. We will put up with impure air if we have to, but we cannot put up with a Yukon blast blowing about our ears continually.

I come often to this chamber when the House is not sitting and I generally find a good many members here so that the difficulty is tp turn on the fans when there are no members. I assure the House that during the recess I will give my best attention to the ventilation of the chamber. I will consult not only my own officers, but men who have acquired experience in that line of business.

I would gather from the statement of my hon. friend from Ilalton (Mr. Henderson) that what the Minister of Public Works does is to turn the fans on against the members of this side of the House so as to kill off the opposition, and that he does not do so on the other side. If there is any truth in that, it is of course taking a most unfair advantage of us.

My hon. friend may rest assured that that side of the House has been blown up enough without me.
Mal i time provinces-General repairs, harbours. rivers and bridges, $8,000.
Is there anything in this vote for the works on Pictou Island, to which I have called attention several times.

The chief engineer informs me that we have taken the amount out of the general vote of last year to do that work and the work is going on now.
Slides and booms-repairs, &c., $10,000.
What is the necessity for this ?

Trade is developing and there are more demands for works of all kind. We make a rough estimate for the general vote. We cannot tell of course whether storms will destroy one wharf or ten wharfs throughout the country and the estimate is always approximate.
But this is for slides and booms. The explanation of the minister is very satisfactory so far as it is definite, but it is not very definite.
These works are quite outside of the ordinary vote. These are revenue bearing woras.
How much revenue do you get ?
I never handle a dollar of the revenue, but I think the revenue reaches about $130,000 a year. These works which pay best are on the St. Maurice and the Ottawa rivers.
The total expenditure is how much ?

So that the work is really paid for out of collections ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS Yes.
Telegraphs Land and cable tel 'graph lines of the sea, coasts and islands of the lower rivers, ana Gulf of St. Lawrence and maritime provinces, including working expenses of vessels required for cable service, $17,000.

This sum is asked for in connection with our cable and telegraph system. We have cables between Anticosti and the north shore, and between the Magdalen Islands and Meat Cove on the Island of Cape Breton, and also in New Brunswick. The steamer ' Newfield ' was wrecked, and we have been obliged to buy another steamer, the 1 Tyrian,' and to equip her, and this sum is asked in connection with that.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if he is prepared to give the House and the country a full statement ais to the policy of the government with respect to the improvement of the telegraph and cable service in the gulf. In view of the lamentable record of losses in the gulf last season, I think we should have a comprehensive statement as to what steps the government are taking to mitigate the evils to which that route has been subject.

I may say that we have completed our telegraph system to Belle Isle. We have laid a cable between Belle Isle and the north shore, and we have equipped two Marconi stations-one on Belle Isle and one on the north shore. When the supplementary estimates come, I think my hon. friend will find that I have not forgotten that important question. I think our telegraph system down by the sea should be completed. I feel that we should be at home, if I may so speak, with our telegraph system, so that it will be connected with all the cables of the continent.

We shall have full explanations from the hon. minister before the supplementary estimates pass ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS Yes.
Has the hon. minister had any communication with the shipping interest on the subject ?
Yes.
I suppose the correspondence will be brought down, so that we may see if anything can be done to effect some improvement in the insurance rates ?

I will bring down all the correspondence I have.
At one o'clock committee took recess. Committee resumed at Three o'clock.
This amount iis asked to supplement last year's vote, it is to pay for accounts that are due.
Is the ' Tyrian ' to be used entirely las a cable steamer 7
Yes.
Have you sufficient work ?
Yes.
How many milesl of cable have you to lay ?
The total mileage of our system is about 0,000 miles, including the Yukon Territory. We have 230 miles of cable to lay.

The hon. minister was kind enough to provide for a new cable between House Harbour and Amherst, Magdalen Islands last year or two years ago. The cable is, I understand, on board a steamer, but has not yeit been laid. Will the hon. gentleman attend to this matter this year, as our telegraphic service there is very poor indeed ?

The cable was purchased in England and has readied Canada, and as soon as the season permits, it will be laid down.
Yukon public buildings, including revote of $23,723.32, lapsed $84,000.

A part of this vote Is composed of a revote, amounting to $23,723. That sum lapsed because the accounts for last year did not reach Ottawa In ibime. The balance of the vote is to cover expenditure incurred on public buildings in the Yukon, besides the appropriation. I,n other words tlie resident engineer, Mr. Fowler, has been obliged to spend more thian he thought on the public buildings out there.

What public
buildings has the government erected in
the Yukon ?

The government house, which is a residence for the commissioner, a building for the post office and custom-house, and administration building, iu which all the branches of the public service are located and a court house. We have several other public buildings in. the Yukon, and I gave the lisit in the previous debate. In the sup-plementaries we have arranged ;in such a way that the Yukon government will have charge of all local business just ias has the government in the North-west Territories, and my department will keep charge only of the federal business, fbhat is to say, the post office and the government house. It would be easier for the Yukon government to take charge of all the local buildings there as they are on the spot and know more about them than I do.
Are there official residences also for the judges ?
No, bivt we pay the rental of the government judges residence.
What are the furnishings ?
We do not furnish the judges house residence, but we bad to provide the furnishings for the buildings I have mentioned.
How is it the hon. gentleman wants $60,000 more than be thought last year would be required ?

It was very difficult to form an accurate estimate of the cost of work in the Yukon, especially when there was no telegraphic communication, and Mr. Fowler, the resident architect, under estimated the cost.
Has the hon. gentleman's department a resident engineer in the Yukon ?
Not now.
These estimates were made, I suppose, in the Yukon and not in Ottawa.

These estimates were sent by Mr. Fuller, who was our resident architect. But the estimates were exceeded. However, Mr. Fuller is here in Ottawa, and if my hon. friend would like to have him before the Public Accounts Committee, there is no reason why be would not do so.
I do not know that there is any need of that but

I was just explaining that the reason why we asked for this vote is that the resident architect exceeded bis appropriation. But be tells us that, these buildings having been commenced, be was bound to complete them.
That is quite right. But what is the vote last year which was exceeded ?

The appropriation last year was $145,000 ; as against this Mr. Fuller has drawn cheques to the amount of $228,947, a deficit of about $84,000, for which I am asking this vote. Of course, out of that, as I have explained, over $23,000 had lapsed from last year's appropriation, so I am really only asking for a vote of $60,000.
I do not quite understand that. If there is a difference of $84,000 between what was estimated and what was expended, how can $23,000 of this be a revote ?
Because the money has not been spent ; the accounts did not come in time.
But I understand the hon. minister to say that cheques were issued for $228,000.

The deputy minister has explained the matter to me, and as I understand it, the appropriation was then exhausted. As a matter of fact before we had telegraph communication we never knew where we were in these matters. Our officers would delay and then the slowness of postal communication would cause further delay. But the case is as I have stated-we had an appropriation of $145,000 against which we have an expenditure of $228,947.
But the vote of last year does not expire until the 1st July next. I do not understand the minister's statement that a portion of the vote has lapsed.
The deputy minister explained that what was exceeded was the vote of last year, and out of this year's vote we have had to pay this $23,000, therefore we are short by that amount on this vote.

Why did not you
get it revoted last session ?
Because, I am informed, the session was over when we learned of it.
Oh, oh.
Of course, I cannot help myself in these matters. The money has to be paid.

I understand now-the lapse is one lap back ; but it seems to be a pretty wide margin of error-$84,000 in $145,000. '
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKSr I grant that.
How were the buildings erected, by tender or by day's work ?
I understand that we gave small contracts for material, and so on, but most of the work was by day's labour.
How would it be possible to have so large an error as that in doing the work in that way ?

1 cannot explain more than I have already done. As I have said, we had a resident architect, a man who has been several years in the department and who was recommended to me as the best man for that work. We controlled the expenditure as much as it was possible to do from this distance, but the appropriation was exceeded. In a country where charwomen are paid $5 a day, money goes pretty fast.
The money goes pretty fast-I am disposed to admit that. But what margin of error does the .minister think we ought to allow in future ?
I am glad to say there will be no more errors in this, because these works have been completed.
What has beeu the total cost of these buildings that the minister has spoken of ?
I find that the total cost of the buildings up to 1st January, 1902. so far as reported to Ottawa, was $297,435.45.
What was the estimate ?

I really cannot say. It is rather difficult to make an estimate out there.
To refund the Yukon local council the balance of their outlay in connection with the construction of the Ogilvie bridge, viz.: $32,403, together with the sum of $15,748.27, advanced by them so as to permit of the Hunker Road being completed ready for traffic in 1901-02	$48,151 31
To pay Palmier Bros., in full and final settlement of all demands in connection with their contract for the construction of a wagon road from Williams Roadhouse to mouth of Gold Run	 19,800 00
What funds do the Yukon local council administer ? Why is there a refund ?

I am not in a position to answer the question as it does not belong to the Department of Public Works. But so far as I can say, they are funds collected from the royalties and so on. Out of their local funds they Hon. Mr. TARTE.
have advanced a sum for roads which we are asked to reimburse to them.
Who had the contract with the government for building this wagon road ?

Messrs. Palmer and Russell bad a contract with the Department of Public Works for the construction of this road. That work was recommended by Mr. Ross, the commissioner, and It was on bis recommendation that the contract was awarded.
What is the length of the road ?
Fifteen miles and a half.
Had you authority from parliament to enter into contract for building that road ?
We had a vote for roads last year.
Is this in excess of that vote ?
It is to complete payment for the construction of that road.
How much was paid before on account of this road ?
We had voted $10,000 before.
Then the road cost $29,800 for 15 miles. Is that right ?
No, the total cost of that road was $31,479, and we have paid $11,000. The length of the road is 16 miles.
There was a contract, apparently, according to the wording of the resolution. What was the amount of the contract ?

The deputy minister reminds me that in point of fact the commissioner was the real party who contracted for the road, with the consent of all the officers. The contract price was $10,418 for the first section ; for the second section, eight miles in round numbers, the contract price was $10,950.80. Then there were extras that Mr. Ross, the commissioner, granted. 1 may say that Mr. Ross being a man of experience, when he went there I asked him to certify all the expenditures for the Department of Public Works. I thought it was safer to have him supervise my own officers, and in everything I am asking from the House to-day I have the sanction and approbation of Mr. Ross.
Were tenders called for by public advertisement ?
Yes.

I desire, Mr. Chairman, to call your attention to the fact that there is so much noise in the Chamber that it is difficult to hear. While the committee is going on in supply we will have to have better order. On Friday evening it was almost impossible to hear the minister who was in charge, and it is very difficult this afternoon. Unless we have better order I shall move that the committee rise.
If I cannot be heard from this side of the House I will go across.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Very frequently when the committee begins work there is a system of interviewing going on in the House. Members gather in little groups around certain seats for the purpose of transacting business, which causes a hum that renders it almost impossible for the average member to hear what is going on. I hope that will be avoided as far as possible.

I may point out to to the minister that on Friday evening he was making a good deal of noise himself while the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were going on. I am glad to see that he is being taught a lesson on the present occasion.
I must apologize for my past faults. I have the best intentions for the future.
I desire to say, Mr. Chairman, that from our seats up here we hear nothing whatever of what is going on down below, and we have to amuse ourselves as best we can.

Tenders were asked for for this work, and thirteen were sent in. The lowest tenderer was a gentleman named Forsyth, but he had to be passed over because his securities went back on him. The next lowest tenderer was Mr. Palmer, the man to whom we gave the contract.
When was the contract let ?
July 27th, 1900.
That was previous to Mr. Ross going in ?
Yes, perhaps so. But he was consulted. I remember very well, when our final settlement took place.
That is the account that Palmer & Russell had a dispute with the department about ?
Yes, there was a difference.
What was the difference ?

There were extras for about $10,000, or $12,000, and as I did not know exactly what to do, I referred the whole thing to Mr. Ross, in whom I had implicit confidence, and he settled with them with the aid of my officers.
That is unfair to the lowest tenderer.

The lowest tenderer was passed over because, before accepting his contract, his securities went back on him, and for no other reason.
Quesneilla Atlin telegraph line-Yukon system, $107,000.
What is the explanation here ?

This money is asked to pay two different accounts. First to pay back accounts incurred in 1899-1900 and also in 1900-1901, amounting to $55,640.09. It is also to pay the cost of the gap that had to be completed during last session. When I came to the House on a previous occasion I stated that we had every reason to believe that the gap to be filled would be about 50 miles long. Of course, this is a wild country, and nobody had ever previously travelled over the ground between Hazelton and Telegraph Creek. Instead of having to complete a gap of 50 miles, we had 111 miles of telegraph line to build. Now, we had to carry our provisions on boats and in other ways, and we had to spend $30,000 to take the men in in the spring and bring them out in the fall. We would seem to have spent $79,000 for that 111 miles of gap, but we have really and practically spent only $49,000 upon that work, as $30,000 had to be spent to take the men in and bring them out again. I am asking this amount of money to pay $55,000 of old accounts and to pay the cost of this gap. During the last winter there were a couple of months in which there were 27 feet of snow. For the next season, as soon as spring is open, I intend buying cable and laying it down so that in the winter months there will be no interruption in the telegraph system.
Why did you not run straight across the country ?
It is altogether out of the question. They were obliged at times before reaching these points to shovel five or six feet of snow on both sides.
At what season of the year?
It was in the month of April that they started. It cost us $30,000 to take them in and bring them out.

I have heard it remarked that in building this line, the engineers or those

who were responsible, ran past one another about 50 miles.
They did not. If my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) will be good enough to look at the map he will find that there was nothing of the kind.
Then it is not the case that they did run past each other ?
I say on the report of the engineers who were there and who are here to-day, on the report of Mr. Boyer, who is a most reliable officer, that nothing of the kind occurred.
My information was that the parties building the line ran past each other about 50 miles.
I am quite sure that information is incorrect, as the map shows.
I am pleased to hear that It is not so.
This map has been prepared by the officers who built this line.

I asked some information from the hon. minister the other evening which he was not then prepared to give. What is the total length of the Yukon telegraph line from Ashcroft to Dawson, the total cost and the number of men employed?

The total length of the Yukon lines, including the Port Simpson to Hazelton branch, is 2,135 miles. Here are the distances : first section, Ashcroft to Quesnelle, including the branch from Ashcroft to Lilloet station and other branches from Quesnelle to Barkerville, 281 miles ; second section, which extends from Quesnelle to Atlin by way of Hazelton and Telegraph Creek, 397 miles; Hazelton to Telegraph Creek, 333 miles; Telegraph Creek to Atlin, 214 miles, making a total distance from Quesnelle to Atlin of 944 miles; branch line from Port Simpson to Hazelton, 200 miles ; Atlin to Dawson, including branch to Cariboo crossing, (ill miles ; branch from Dawson to the American boundary, 97 miles, making in all -2,135 miles.
What is the total cost ?
$786,224.41 not including $94,000 for supplies and provisions which were left at the different camps on different occasions, and which have been paid out of construction money.
Does that include this estimate ?

Yes, the total estimate. If the total sum of Mr. BOYD.
$7S6,224.41 is divided by the total mileage of 2,135 miles, then the general cost per mile would be $368.23, and If the House wants -to know how much per mile was the cost on the different sections I am prepared to give it.
How many telegraph offices have you ?
We have 70 offices including refuge houses and about 119 employees.
What kind of wire did you use ?

No. 8 wire. As I have said, next winter season we contemplate laying a cable on the most difficult part of the line so as to avoid the great damages caused by the storms. Between Hazelton and Telegraph Creek last winter there were 27 feet of snow, which accounts for the interruption in the service. We expect that by using the new device we will be able to have an uninterrupted service the whole winter round. The cost of the different sections of the line is as follows :
From Ashcroft to Barkerville 281 miles, less 62 miles to Lilloet making 219 miles ; total cost $24,000 or $110 per mile.
From Quesnelle to Atlin 944 miles, total cost $500,494.75, or $540.77 per mile.
From Fort Simpson to Hazelton 200 miles, total cost $64,037.52, or $323.18 per mile.
Atlin to Dawson including brancn to Bennett 637 miles, total cost $178,480.53 ; cost per mile $280.19.
From Dawson to the boundary, 95 mues, total cost $18,611.39, or $195.90 per mile.
On which section did one of the civil servants in the employ of the government contract with the government to supply the poles.
The Bennett and Dawson line.
Had any civil servants contracts on any other sections ?

I do not admit that a civil servant had a contract at all, because Mr. Rochester is not a civil servant. He was a temporary employee for a time. I have already explained to the House how this matter happened. Mr. Rochester started from Ottawa and the intention of Mr. Charleson was that Mr. Rochester who had long experience was to be employed as foreman of works. AVhen he had been a few months there he contracted for the poles. We were then paying $3 for the poles and he offered to supply tnem for $2. Mr. Charleson rightly or wrongly accepted his offer, and after his contract was completed he began again as foreman

lof construction. Let me say at once that Mr. Richardson who was then in charge of the construction of the line was the gentleman who accepted all the poles from Mr. Rochester. These are the facts as they are.
I asked the other evening a question with regard to the amount of business done by that telegraph line. Can the minister tell us the amount of messages and the revenue received ?

The revenue since the 1st of July, 1901, has been as follows:	July,	$7,478.78;
August, $7,583.52; September, $8,904.13; October. $8,976.10; November, $6,670.83; December, $6,509.36; January, 1902, $6,950.48; February, $7,683.71; March, $8,898. I may remark that the line was interrupted for several weeks, otherwise I suppose our receipts would have been larger.
Can you tell me what proportion otf the revenue is derived from the government service, and what proportion from general business ?

This is our net revenue. For next year we expect a revenue of $125,000 at least. The expenditure during the last six months or a year has been very large, because we were still building. We shall be able to reduce the expenditure very largely.
Will you be able to reduce your rates ? The impression is that if the rates were lowered to a reasonable figure, the business would be very greatly increased.
What are the rates?

I think they are about $4.75 for ten words from Victoria or Vancouver to the Yukon. I am informed that if a message is sent from Ashcroft to London, the full Yukon rate is added to the cable rate, whereas in cabling over any other line there is only the usual local rate added to the cable rate. I understand that in cabling anywhere along the government line, the full Yukon rate is added to the cable rate.

Of course, I would be only too glad, if possible, to reduce the rates. We have not had many complaints. The rates, I grant, are not low; but that line has cost a large amount of money, and the rates must be judged according to local circumstances. Everything is high out there.

But that does not affect the case I mention. If you telegraph from' Ashcroft to Victoria the rate is perhaps 50 cents; but if you cable from Ashcroft to London, the full Yukon rate is added to the cable rate.

Is the hon, gentleman sure of that ?
Mi-. EARLE. I have been told so by a party who has cabled.
I am glad ,my hon. friend has called my attention to that. I will immediately look Into it.
What class of instruments are used in those seventy offices ? Are they repeaters, or can the hon. gentleman give me some idea of what batteries are used ?

I have not the prices of the instruments here, but if my hon. friend wants them,
I will .give them with pleasure.

The average cosit of that line is $368.23 per male, with offices about 30 m'iles apart. In Manitoba it costs about $150 a mile to build and equip a telegraph line with offices about 10 miles apart, although we have to bring the telegraph poles three or four hundred miles. This line must have been built through a wooded country where the telegraph poles must have been very near. In the district of Keewiatin you can get large cedar telegraph poles at 50 or 75 cents. What kind of poles were these, which cost $2 each ?
I do not think we could have used cedar there. We had to use the native timber.
How could the poles cost $2 each ?

The cost of transportation has been the greatest expense. Some parts of the work have not cost even $150 a mile. For instance, that part of the work from Ashcroft to Barkerville cost only $110 a mile. In other words, in a civilized country it did not cost nearly so much. The last gap cost over $700 a mile, because we had to pack provisions, wires, and so on, for a distance of 100 miles, and in some cases the men had to shovel away snow and ice to a depth of 6 feet.
What wages are paid the operators and what are their duties ?

The average price paid was between $80 per month and three dollars a day. I am speaking of the whole staff. For the coming year we have reduced the wages. The line was opened in a very hasty way, and we have reduced all the salaries, so that I expect next year the expenditure will be about $125,000.

The cost of the poles appears to have been $2. I understand that there are no great transportation charges because they were floated down the river. I hope that the hon. minister does not approve of officials of the government taking contracts of this kind. I understand that the contractor was on salary before he took this

contract and that after lie completed the contract, he went hack on salary again and has been in the employ of the government ever since. I also understand that while he was carrying on the contract he kept the books of the government. I hope the hon. gentleman has taken steps to find out what the poles really cost, because the government would be entitled to the profits, the contractor being an official of the government. A civil servant has no right to take government contracts, and the officials implicated should be severely reprimanded.

I am not prepared to admit that Mr. Charle-son did right in giving Mr. Rochester this contract. I told him that if I had been in his place I would not have done it. But we must look into the circumstances. Our employes were in a wild country. The poles had been supplied to Mr. Charleson by the Victoria Trading Company for the line between Bennett and Caribou Crossing at $3 each. Mr. Rochester who has been employed in bush operations all his life, offered to supply the poles for the remainder of the work between Bennett and Dawson for $2 each, and Mr. Charleson gave him the contract at that price. My hon. friend is not quite correct in saying that Mr. Rochester continued in the employ of the government while he was earrving out this contract.
He kept the books.

My hon. friend should be fair. Mr. Charleson was alone and had no bookkeeper. Mr. Rochester is a first-class bookkeeper, as my hon. friend knows, because he heard Mr. Rochester give his evidence before the Public Accounts Committee. Mr. Charleson had no other man to keep his books, and Mr. Rochester agreed to keep them free of charge while carrying out his contract. He kept the books at night. I do not say that that was right or regular. But I say there has been no stealing, so far as I can see. I think that Mr. Charleson should not have employed him. I would not have done so, because I would have anticipated criticism, and of course fair criticism, but the facts are as I have stated.
Could not Mr. Rochester have bought the poles for the government instead of Mi-. Charleson ?

1 am not prepared to agree to that. My hon. friend and myself are pretty able men, but if we would venture to start a trade in poles, I think we would lose a good deal of money and a good deal of prestige-both of which we require.
Mr. Rochester was bookkeeper for the government and resigned his position to become a contractor. That is to say, he did not draw any pay as bookkeeper after he had contracted to furnish
the poles for $2 apiece. Would it not have been 'just ns easy and much better for the country if Mr. Rochester had bought the poles for the government at $2 apiece instead of Mr. Charleson.

If he had bought the poles for the government, I would not be obliged to give the explanations I am now giving. But I cannot help it. The poles were bought and paid for and I cannot do any thing more. I told Charleson that he could have spared me all that trouble if he had acted differently.
How much increase in salary did Mr. Rochester get after the contract was completed ?

He did not get any increase until the next spring when he had full charge of the work, which was more difficult in that wild place than it was between Bennett and Dawson. That increase of salary was not kept very long for I reduced it as soon as I learned of it.
The minister has told us that he reprimanded Mr. Charleson for this transaction. Did he reprimand him by letter or verbally ?

When Mr. Charleson came back. I told him that he had not done what I would have done. He said he had not done anything wrong and had done for the best, but I told him that it would give me a great deal of trouble to defend him as I am now doing.
Do you save .$1 a pole on the price ?
From what I could learn, I really believe the price was a fair one.
You have not learned what class of wood was in those poles and the size.

It could only have been the kind of wood that grows in that country-a kind of spruce,
I understand.
You will have to replace the poles inside of three years.
1 am sure my hon. friend would not advise me to import the wood.
What was the diameter of the bulk and the height.
I cannot tell you that.
I was only curious to know how it was the minister came to the conclusion that the price was a fair one, since he does not know the kind of pole or its size or its height.

1 have not the very best information. The gentleman who was in charge of construction is a Mr. Richardson, who is an employee of the Canadian Pacific Railway on their telegraph line. He has built nearly all their lines, and it was because he was an experienced man that I instructed him to supervise the structure of our work. He came back and, of course, I asked him for all possible information and he told me the price was fair. He was before the Public Accounts Committee last session, and 1 think he made that statement.

It would be desirable to know whether he was aware of the size of the poles at the butt, their height and material. If he did not know anything more about it than the hon. minister seems to know, his opinion would not be of much value. In what particular section was it that Mr. Rochester supplied the poles ?

It may be true that my opinion on these matters is not of much value, but Mr. Richardson was on the spot and received the poles, and he has been a telegraph constructor all his life. The section for which Mr. Rochester supplied the poles was between Bennett and Dawson City.

The hon. minister has spoken of the difficulty of getting in supplies, explaining that in one section it cost $30,000 to take in the men and their supplies to the ground and back. Would the same difficulty exist on this portion of the line ?
No, not so much.
Where would the supplies come from ?
The supplies would come from Vancouver.
From whom were the supplies bought and how were they purchased ?
I cannot say at the moment how it is done this year, but last year and the year before they were bought by tender.

My information is entirely different-that there was no tender asked for a dollar's worth of supplies that went to the Yukon, either for the Public Works or for any other department, and that, moreover, this business was peddled out, as was done some years ago.
I remember distinctly that the last time we discussed this matter in the House, it was shown very clearly that tenders were asked for groceries and provisions.
Where ?
In British Columbia.
I am positive that that information is incorrect.
I am corrected by my deputy minister, who tells me that circulars were issued and that we got eighteen tenders and that out of these eighteen tenders Kelly, Douglas & Company were the lowest.

My information is that the very opposite of that, even that firms contemporary with Messrs. Kelly, Douglas & Company, in Vancouver, including many Liberals, who declare that supplies were bought regardless of tenders, and that they were given no opportunity to get the business. I am as positive as I am standing here that that is correct.

The information from my officials is what I have given-that tenders were called for and Messrs. Kelly, Douglas & Company were the lowest, and that since then, provisions have been bought at this lowest tender price. It happened that I was away when these circulars were sent out, although, of course, I am responsible for all that has been done. But I am sure that my officer would not make a mistake upon this point, and that tenders were asked for and that they were asked for exactly as my hon. friend (Mr. Earle) would do. In his large business he would not advertise for tenders, except in the way we did. I do not say that it is right or that it is wrong; I am only giving the facts.
Were there eighteen tenders from eighteen different firms ?
Yes.

I have some recollection of the discussion, and I think the information furnished was that a number of circulars were sent out. I believe 1 was consulted, when they were sent out, as the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) was away, and the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock), who was acting Minister of Public Works, was also absent at the time. I think these circulars were sent to parties in Victoria, Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, and some cities in the east. I am sure that my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Earle) will find that that statement, as regards the original purchase of groceries, is entirely correct.

It may be, and I hope it is. But my information 'is different. Not only from my own knowledge of the business there, but from the statements of par! ties in the trade in Vancouver, some of

them life-long Liberals, who complain very bitterly about it. It is a well known fact that everything is carried to Messrs. Kell}', Douglas & Company.
It was not so in the original purchase ; as to later purchases, I do not pretend to be informed. In the original purchase circulars were sent out, as I have stated.
But I am speaking of the purchase of supplies for the telegraph line for this year 1902.
I understand that Mr. Charleson has bought his supplies at the same prices that were quoted by Messrs. Kelly, Douglas & Company when the former tenders were given.
When were the original tenders asked for ?
In 1899, I suppose-I was away.
Three years ago ?
Two years ago.
Prices have changed since the tenders were asked for.
Prices of provisions have not lowered.
They certainly have lowered in some cases.

What prices have lowered

sugar ? Or bacon ?
Flour and many other articles. Is it not customary to ask for tenders each year ?

I have the figures now under my hand, and I save my neck once more. Here are the people from whom we bought provisions last year : Messrs. Kelly, Douglas & Company, $5,908; the Hudson's Bay Company, $7,655; Messrs. J. Y. Galbraith, Telegraph Creek, $4,265; Messrs. Cunningham & Son, $4,220; and other small purchases- these are for provisions. Hardware seems to have been bought right and left.
These are dealers in the interior, except Messrs. Kelly, Douglas & Company.
Kelly, Douglas & Company have only a limited amount
The accounts are not all in yet up to the 30th June.
I have here the figures up to the completion up to 31st January, 1902.
Is it the intention to continue buying supplies for the current year on the same contract ?
No.
The hon. gentleman will ask for new tenders.

I will say to the House that I intend to change the system under which we have bought in the past. I am going to try to get quotations, as has been suggested to me by some hon. gentlemen in the House, and ask people to sell on those quotations. I shall be very glad to welcome suggestions from hon. gentlemen on. either side of the House as to the best way of purchasing.

Do I understand from the minister that in future tenders will be asked from people who are in business regardless of politics ? I do not mean advertised tenders necessarily, because sometimes the purchases are so small it would not pay to advertise. But in oases where a fair amount of purchases are to be made, will the minister authorize requisitions to be sent to firms in the different localities, regardless of polities, and let them quote their prices, and will he accept the lowest tenderer ?
No, no. Country first.
Other things being equal. That is my duty.
Country first.

I am speaking of patronage. There are a great many good men in both parties, and I find there are enough good men in the Liberal party to supply the government in many lines at the lowest prices. I may, however, mention to my hon. friend that on many occasions in the past I have asked for tenders and quotations from men who differ with me in politics. I am prepared to appeal for the 'truth of my statement, to the lists of my purchases from Montreal and Toronto, especially from Montreal, where I have asked for quotations, for instance, for hardware, for boilers, and things like that. My instructions to our officers are :	When you find enough competition in the Liberal party, our duty is to stand by the party; but when you cannot, then go outside the party. I have done so repeatedly, and I will do it again. We are asking for tenders for nearly all the works, and the lowest tenderer invari-

ably gets the contract, in my department, at any rate. But let me add that I will change t.o a large extent the mode of purchasing. I am willing to meet the trade, and I will improve on my predecessors, on myself even. I (have just instructed my officers very lately to purchase direct from the manufacturer. That is a good policy to follow.

I am afraid the minister has qualified his first statement to such an extent that the country will get no benefit. Now there are many friend's of the government who support the government in election times, who are in business in a wholesale way, but they don't happen to come to Ottawa and go about the departmental buildings here, bothering the ministers to secure contracts. But if a requisition was sent to them they would be very glad to quote prices. Then there is another class of people who come to Ottawa and lobby and work among the different departments, and the minister must know they come. They are a class of people who are not able to sell at the lowest prices, but WhOi through their influence in many ways, are able to get orders. The other class to which I have referred are doing business in a wholesale way, and although they may be supporters of the government, I know as a matter o,f fact that some of them never get an opportunity of quoting. It is frequently the men who are not in as good a position to quote low prices that get the business, because of their persistence in visiting the offices and presenting their claims upon the government, telling what they have done for them, in this election or that election, or what they will do, or some other nonsensical thing. I would strongly urge upon the minister" to qualify his last statement, and to send out requisitions broadcast to business firms regardless of their politics.

I am willing to make an appointment with my hon. friend for next session, and i'f I do not convince him that I have bought at the lowest possible prices of tbe market, I want him to tell me.
Mr. REID (Grenville. The minister is not quite so good as the Postmaster General, who, when he advertises for tenders for the mail service, gives tbe contract to tbe lowest tenderer irrespective of politics.
I do the same thing in every public contract.

The hon. gentleman must know that we are all in politics, all of us. We are playing the game the best we can. When I'ask for public tenders for public buildings, for a wharf, a breakwater, or any other important work, I always accept the lowest tenderer. I challenge any man from either side of the House to point to a single case in my department where I have not awarded the contract to the lowest tenderer, whether he is a Conservative or a Liberal. For doing this some of my friends on this side of the House have called me an old Tory. Now, I am accused of being bad because I do nott give everything to. my hon. friends opposite. Why, they have been eighteen years in office, and it is time that the poor Liberals who were so long in the cold shades of opposition should now (have a little show. But my hon. friends, opposite when they cross the floor of the House, will do just as I have been doing, and if they do not do worse, it will be a blessing of Providence.
What was the average cost of the poles for the whole line?
We have not bought any poles except on that section, because our men made most of the poles themselves.

There must be some idea of what they cost, because the reason advanced by the hon. minister was that Rochester could get them for $2 each, and that the cost had been $3 each at some particular time. If you know they cost $3 each, you must know what they cost on each section. You have the same information in regard to each section.

There was an arrangement for a small part of the line with the Victoria Grading Company. We were to pay them $3 per pole, but that arrangement was cancelled and Mr. Rochester got the contract at $2 per pole. Later ou, instead of going on with that subcontract, the men made the poles as they went along with the work. But my hon. friend must not lose sight of the fact that all of the sections were not alike. A mile of telegraph line in the gap we filled last year cost more than a mile elsewhere. It is quite impossible to give the price of each pole, because, suppose we bad fifty or one hundred, or two hundred men carrying on this work it is impossible to be able to say that a pole here or elsewhere, would cost so much. These men were paid by tlie day and they were doing their work.
Was it only on the line between Dawson and Bennett that poles were obtained by contract ?
Yes.
How many were purchased at $2 and how many at $3 ?

We got 330 from the Victoria Grading Com-panv at $3, and it was proved before the Public Accounts Committee that the number of poles supplied for the balance of the line between Dawson and Bennett was 6,000.
Were not tenders called for in respect to those that were supplied by the Victoria Grading Company?
I understand not.
Where did Mr. Rochester get those which he supplied?
I cannot say.
The hon. gentleman has no information whatever as to where Mr. Rochester got those poles?

None, except that Mr. Rochester, in the Public Accounts Committee, said that he made a sub-contract with Mr. Johnston. He admitted that. Beyond that I cannot say where the poles came from. I do not know.
At what price were they to be delivered by the sub-contractor to Mr. Rochester?
I do not know. I have no right to know, either.
Who was the sub-contractor ?
Johnston, I understand.
Where does he live?
I do not know. I have never met him.
Did Charleson call for tenders before he awarded this contract to Rochester?
No.
And the hon. gentleman thinks that is a proper course?

Asking for tenders under the circumstances might have been difficult, but all the same, I say again-I have nothing to hide-Mr. Charleson might have avoided giving that contract to Mr. Rochester. It is not necessary to repeat it. I admit, although I believe that the price, if I have been rightly informed by those who have been on the
spot, and by Mr. Richardson, who is a very competent man, was reasonable.
What was Richardson doing there ?
He was supervising the construction of the line.
For whom ?
For the government.
Under the control of Charleson ?

No, Charleson was at that time a kind of general officer, not only for the completion of the telegraph line, but for works elsewhere and Richardson was in charge of the construction of the telegraph line.
That would mean that he was foreman of construction for a portion of the line under Charleson.
No.
And took orders from Charleson ?
Charleson was a superior officer. Richardson would be in the position of my chief engineer here in relation to myself.
Do you make them do what you want ?
No, I hare never tried to make them do wrong.
I would not suggest that the hon. minister would try to make them do wrong.
The hon. minister says we have no right to know the price at which Johnston supplied poles to Roenester. Why have we not a right to know that ?

For a very simple reason.
