My hon. friend is a lawyer and he has factums to be printed; suppose that he comes to ' La Pat-rie ' office when he has a Montreal case, and we would be glad to see him there, he will give us a contract for the printing of the factum. Suppose that my sons gave to another printing office the work of printing the factum, that they sub-let the contract, he would have no right to know how much they paid for getting the work done. It happens every day in the Department of Public Works that we give a contract for a public building, for a bridge, or some other public work and the contractor gives a sub-contract. What right have I to ask this contractor how much he has paid for his material ? I have no right to do that. The

contract is given and the contractor buys his stone, his iron or his timber and we have no right to know how much he pays for it. In this case the principle is absolutely the same.
How long after Rochester left the service of the government was it before this arrangement was made with him ?

He left the service of the department-he did not leave the service, but he did so for two or three months when he got that contract. He carried out his contract and then resumed his position as foreman.
It is something like Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.
Comparisons are odious.
My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) suggests that it was odorous. As a matter of fact this contract was made while he was in the employ of the government, under salary.

No, he left the employ of the department, even the ablest lawyer cannot mix me up on occasions like this. He cannot do it. That man took the contract and carried it out at $2 per pole. While he was carrying out that contract he did not get a dollar from the Department of Public Works. That is the whole case.
Did Rochester, the contractor, inspect the poles furnished by him on behalf of the government ?

No, I said repeatedly and it has been proven in the Public Accounts Committee that Rochester had nothing to do with the inspection of the poles. Richardson inspected them. The thing was done in the ordinary way of business, and although I say it again, it should not have been done, because we would not have had all this discussion and it would have been regular if it had been done in some other way.
Are these people still in your employ ?
No, Richardson is not in the service of the government.
Richardson or Rochester ?
Rochester is just completing our accounts.
And Charleson ?
Richardson and Charleson are just completing the accounts of this line.
On what date did Mr. Rochester leave the government service.
It was established before the Public Accounts Committee, but I cannot remember now.

Of course this is not the Public Accounts Committee and when the minister is putting through his estimates I should like to know the facts. There was some negotiation for the supply of these poles, and while that negotiation was going on between Mr. Rochester and Mr. Charleson was not Mr. Rochester in the employ of the government ?
I suppose he was.

Well, that is perfectly frank. Then the position is, that Mr. Charleson who was superintending the building of this line for the government entered into a negotiation with an officer in the employ of the government for the supply of these poles at $2 a piece, and eventually he awarded a contract for some 6,000 poles to Mr. Rochester without asking for tenders from any other person. The minister does not know officially or otherwise at what price these poles were supplied to Mr. Rochester by the sub-contractor.
No.
I suppose that Mr. Rochester had not much to do with getting these poles out and matters of that kind. What was Mr. Rochester doing while this contract was being carried out by the sub-contractor.
Mr. Rochester was the contractor and he gave a sub-contract and I suppose he was looking after the delivery of the poles on his own account.
Did not the subcontractor cover everything that he was obliged to do.

Yes, but we had nothing at all to do with that man. Mr. Rochester was our contractor and I suppose he had to see that the goods were delivered. They were not moved after they were delivered to Mr. Rochester by the sub-contractor.
No, but Mr. Rochester was our contractor and he was obliged to see that he delivered the goods. I was not watching over it myself.
Perhaps it would be better if the minister had been watching over it.
Oh, he did not steal any poles.

I really do not understand yet what Mr. Rochester was doing.
o
Mr. Rochester had to look after the construction of the whole line and the poles are only a part of that.
At what particular date of the negotiation did Mr. Rochester leave the employment of the government so as to cease drawing a salary.
The Deputy Minister tells me that he thinks Mr. Rochester left the service in the beginning of May and the contract was made then.
Made on the day on which he left the service.
I suppose so.
When did he resume.
In October.
That was the date when the poles had been delivered.
I suppose so.
Did he resume in the same position and at the same salary and for the performance of the same duties.
I am informed that he resumed service at the same salary.

As a matter of fact it amounts to this, does it not-if I am wrong the minister will correct me That Mr. Rochester remained there from the 1st of May until October, and instead of drawing a salary he took his profit off these poles.
There is no doubt about that.
That is about the substance of it.

Yes, it is the substance of it.
Mx-. BOitDEN (Halifax). For the matter of appearance he did not draw his salary during the time he was making a profit because of course he could not receive both- that is right I suppose.
He did not draw his salary.
But he had charge of the books in the mean time.

As there was no other bookkeeper on the spot and as he opened the books he agreed to work at night on the books without charging a dollar to us. What my hon. friend says is perfectly true. From May to
October instead of being employed as an employee of the department he acted as a contractor.
When were the first poles delivered under the sub-contract by Mr. Johnston.
Upon my word I don't know.
Perhaps the minister will find out from his officer.
I will be only too glad to get the information.
How long did Mr. Rochester remain in the employ of the government in that same position after the sub-contract was performed.

He is still in our employ. He remained as foreman of works until the whole work was completed, and I may say in passing that Mr. Rochester has proved to be a very able man and in spite of what is being said here to-day-
You had a thoroughly practical man independent of him.

Let me finish the sentence. In spite of what has been said here to-day I think Mr. Rochester is such an able man that he can be employed for some other work. He is an energetic man and a sober man. Of course when I learned that a sub-contract had been given I took special care to go through his accounts and the whole work, and I make bold to say, unless I make a very great mistake indeed, he is a thoroughly honourable man and able too.
I have not made any criticism so far either on his ability or upon his honour. What was his salary, and what were his duties, and what were his living expenses before this contract was entered into ?
His salary was $200 a month, and I understand that they had no living allowance, but lived together in a mess under canvas which they thought was the best way. He was foreman of works.
What did that involve.
It involved construction under Mr. Richardson.
Did he continue to mess in the camp with the rest while the contract was going on ?
I do not know.
Perhaps the minister would be able to find it out from his officer.
I will get the information. 1 would not be surprised if he continued in the mess as he was keeping accounts for us without charge.

Yes, but he had full charge when Mr. Richardson left. Mr. Richardson constructed only that part of the line between Dawson and Bennett, and Mr. Rochester had full charge of the work in the more difficult part of the country and received more pay. I may say that when I found that I reduced his salary myself later on.
That was in 1900?
Yes.
From October last it was reduced to $200 a month ?
Yes.
What is he getting now in the city of Ottawa ?
$200 a month, but no allowance. He will not be employed for more than a week or so now.
Has Mr. Charle-son given any explanation why he did not ask tenders from any one but his own officials ?
No, he has not.
Has the minister asked for any explanation ?

I asked Mr. Charieson why he gave the contract to Mr. Rochester, and he said it was the best bargain he could have made. Suppose we had asked for tenders. The line was built in the summer, and there was great pressure to get the work finished. It would have taken 3 or 4 weeks to get tenders, and the result might have been that the line would not have been completed that year. W'ould my hon. friend advise such a course ? In those days papers were scarce in the Yukon.
There would not seem to have been great difficulty in asking for tenders from all the employees in the government, if it was a proper thing to do.
All the employees were not capable of making poles. A bushman is better qualified for that work than others.
That only shows how absurd and wrong the whole thing was.

I must protest against that statement of my hon. friend. No minister could possibly control the expenditure or the work on this telegraph line, owing to the want of means of communication. To-day such a thing could not happen. If I had been informed then that Mr. Charieson had given a contract to one of his employees, I would have told him it was wrong, as I did tell him when he came here. But that does not show that any wrong was done, though it was a wrong proceeding.

Yes, and I have not the slightest doubt, on the minister's statement to-day, that the government could recover every dollar of profit Mr. Rochester made on the contract. I believe that Mr. Charieson had no authority from the government to give a contract to one of his employees, and I have not the slightest doubt that this government has the right to every dollar of profit he made, although I know that two ministers of the Crown have prevented that information being brought before the public in the Public Accounts Committee. Unless Mr. Charieson possessed extraordinary powers, beyond those which any man in his position should possess, he could not have made this pretended contract with one of his employees, without any outside competition at all, and then have the man go through the form of leaving the public service when as a matter of fact he remained in it, as the minister admitted to-day; but, instead of receiving a salary during that time, he was doing very much better by making a large profit out of this contract created in this very indefensible way.
How does my hon. friend know that Mr. Rochester made a large profit ?
Shall I tell the hon. gentleman ?
With pleasure.

Because the hon. gentleman and his colleagues refused to allow that question to be asked in the Public Accounts Committee and suggested to the witness that he need not answer it, which leads me to suppose that they did not want the facts to come out; because I understood that the objection came, not from Mr. Rochester himself, but from two of the ministers.

If that is the only ground on which the hon. gentleman bases his statement, it is baseless. In the Public Accounts Committee there are rules, and it is the duty of the ministers of

the Crown to see that they are followed.
1 have been here a good many years, both as a newspaper man and as a member of parliament, and never have I known a question to be asked as to the prices paid to sub-contractors. My hon. friend has no right to say that ministers of the Crown have prevented rightful information being given. We have followed the ordinary rules of evidence. Nor has my hon. friend any right to state that Mr. Rochester has made large profits. But if he has, does that prove that Mr. Charleson made a bad bargain ? Not by any means. A man may make a large profit on a government contract, and the government may make a good bargain at the same time. The proceeding was not right; I am not going to say that it was. I would not defend it. I told Mr. Charleson in a very firm manner what I say now. It should not have taken place, but all the same there is no evidence that the bargain was a bad one. At the same time, let my hon. friend admit that he has no ground for stating that we have prevented rightful evidence being given in the committee, because we have followed the ordinary rules of evidence.
What was the objection to this evidence ?
The objection to it was the objection of the witness himself.
After it was first suggested to him.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; he was not there, while I was. Mr. Rochester made the objection first, and the chairman ruled. At the next meeting of the committee, the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) tried, in an insidious way, in his able way, to induce the witness to go back on the ruling of the chairman, and then we said,
* Mr. Rochester, you are not obliged to answer.' But Mr. Rochester had first declined to answer, on the ground, which was well taken, that it was his own private affair. Before a court of justice my hon. friend would take the same ground; he cannot deny it; and he would be sustained by any court in the land.

If I had anything to do [DOT]with it, I would probably have a judicial inquiry and ascertain the rights of the parties in a court below. In that case Mr. Rochester would probably find that he would have to answer this question without very much discussion before the judge who tried the case. The minister may be right as to who first took the objection. I was informed the opposite; but I do not know, as I was not there. It does not make the slightest difference, however, whether the facts as to what took place on the first occasion are as the hon. gentleman says or not. There is no doubt at all, according to the min-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
ister's own statement, that upon the question being put, he, himself, and another minister of the Crown suggested to Mr. Rochester that he was not obliged to answer. It was perfectly proper for Mr. Rochester to answer, as far as he is concerned, if he chose, and I do not see why a minister of the Crown should suggest to him that he should refuse to answer. I do not see any special reason why ministers of the Crown, in a matter of this kind, should act as the advocates of an officer of the Crown, who had taken a contract from the government under these very extraordinary circumstances.

When a witness is examined before a committee, I see no objection to any member of the committee saying to the witness that he was not obliged to answer a question put to him. A witness who is a layman, and who is being examined by a lawyer, may be under the impression that he is compelled to answer every question, but I see no harm in any member of the committee putting him right.
What particular harm would there have been in his answering the question.
That was for him to say.

It was a perfectly fair transaction according to the Minister of Public Works, although he admits that it is one which should not have been entered into. But if it was a perfectly fail-contract between the government and Mr. Rochester, what special detriment could there have been to Mr. Rochester's interests in answering the question ?

There was no objection to Mr. Rochester answering any question relating to his contract with the government, but the point was whether he was obliged to answer a question as to what his own sub-contract with another party was, which was quite a different matter.

I wish to refer again to the salary of the operators. Tne hon. minister has told us that those employees are now receiving $80 per month, and that it is his intention to reduce their pay. Considering the cost of this work and the reasons given for the enormous expenditure, I think that instead of lowering the wages of those operators, their pay should be increased. I do not hesitate to say that telegraph operators working in that country should receive a higher salary than $80 per month. Only a night or two ago, a judge in the Yukon district was given $5,000 as a living allowance on account of the expense of living there, and considering this large sum allowed one man for living expenses, it seems to me that an operator ought to be

paid $150 a month and his board. The hon. minister admits the charwomen get $5 a day, and the Auditor General's report shows that an ordinary labourer there gets $4 a day, and that Mr. Rochester got $15 a day, and yet we have skilled men, men doing, not ordinary labour, but expert labour, getting only $80 per month, and we are told that they are to get less in the future. I do not think that that pay is sufficient, considering the country they are working in. It takes longer to learn to be an expert operator tnan to be a judge, and the $5,000 living allowance given to one judge would give each of these seventy operators $70 per month extra, and I say that they should receive it. There was evidently no scarcity' of money for the purpose of construction. The construction has cost one-third more than it should, and I am perfectly satisfied, after watching the Minister of Public Works, that he is not satisfied with himself, for ne has hau to get another member of the cabinet to defend his expenditure. And notwithstanding the enormous cost of construction and all that, the minister is not able to tell us what kind of poles have been used and their size. Had the poles to be brought a long distance, there might be some excuse, but they were cut along the line. Every one employed in the work of construction evidently was paid whatever wages he saw fit to ask, but we are to pay skilled expert labour only $80 a month, and that pay is to be reduced. Then the hon. member for Victoria asked what were the averaged earnings and we were told $7,000 per month. Is that the gross earnings and does it include the telegraphing of the government ?
My hon. friend is of the opinion that the telegraph operators are not paid sufficiently at ->oo a month, but he must not forget that those men are lodged and provisioned.
I know all that.
AVe must also not forget that we have no trouble getting telegraph operators at that rate.
Nor would you have any trouble getting judges at $5,000 a year either.

I would be very much surprised if, when we can get operators at $80 a month, I would be complimented by hon. gentlemen opposite for deciding, out of the kindness of my' heart, to give them $150 a month. I am perfectly sure that I would be censured for doing that. AVe did not compel these men to go there. They went of their own sweet will and are glad to remain at the wages I have mentioned besides lodging and provision. As regards the size of the poles, the diameter of the butts is between nine and ten inches, the diameter of the top is five inches, and the length 22 feet.
Are the operators paid $80 per month and their board and all expenses.
Yes.	[DOT]

When did Air. Richardson, who had charge of the construction of the line, enter the employ of the government, and when did he leave ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC AVOnKS. He entered in March, 1899, at the very beginning of the work between Dawson and Bennett, and left in October, 1899.
Was he in the employ of the government when these poles were purchased from Mr. Rochester.
Yes, and accepted delivery of them all.
Is it a fact that the minister is paying labourers $4 a day and their board.
I cannot really say, but the hon. gentleman must remember that while the operators are employed by the year, the labourers may be only employed for a month or two.
If the operator is a married man, does he get provisions for his family ?

No, we only give a certain quantity of provisions to each man.
Mr. 'BORDEN (Halifax). What was the cost of operation ?

The cost of operation this year would be large. When the supplementary estimates for this year come down I will apply' for the necessary amount to meet this expenditure, and then, if my hon. friend desires I will give him all the information.
That will be all right. The hon. minister mentioned the item of revenue-$20,000 a month, as I understood.
No, $8,890, or something like that, for the month of March.
Does that include messages sent by the departments of giovernment ?
Yes.
Apart from that, what is the revenue ?
I have no statement to show that, but if my hou. friend wants it, I will get it.
That also can be given on the supplementary estimates '?
I can hardly promise that, as the figures will be a little difficult to get.
I suppose the hon. minister has not the data here, and will have to send for them ?

The question having been asked, I will take care, next year to have detailed statements of the revenue. And, ais we lire discussing that point, I would like very much to know the feeling of the House as to the rates. Am I expected to make a paying business out of these lines ? I think I can do so, if I maintain the rates as they are now. I do- not wish to be judged, so far as the working of the (line is concerned, by last year, 'because that was the first year, and every one connected with such matters knows that the first year, is, so to speak, only a construction year. But in future I think I could make a paying business by charging the present rates. This is not a party question, and I would like to know the views of the House upon It.
Can the hon. minister tell ns even roughly, what part of the revenue is from government, and What part of it from private business ?
Of the revenue, of last month, I am quite sure, departmental business cuts a very small figure indeed.

What are we to understand by the statement of the minister that he could make this a paying business V Does he mean to pay something over expenses, or to pay expenses and interest on the capital expenditure as well ?
If I make lit pay interest on the capital with a balance to the good, I think that will he all right.
Certainly.

There is an opportunity for a great object lesson here. There were great difficulties to be overcome-there is no doubt about it-in the construction of that line, as there are in maintaining it in an efficient condition. The obstacles are so great that, as I understand it, the minister intends to have a cable laid to overcome the difficulty of snow on a part of the line. It seems to me that he ought to charge only such rates as are necessary to yield a revenue that will pay working expenses and interest on the indebtedness. If the government can do that and can give us a low rate-low considering the conditions-it will be, as I say, a great object lesson, and will be an argument in favour of the government taking over all the telegraphs of the country.

I would he glad if tine House would give Mr. BORDEN (Halifaxl.
its attention to the telegraph system in British Columbia and the Yukon. We have constructed 2,135 miles of telegraph in the Yukon, and also have a certain number of miles in British Columbia. From Nanaimo to the coast, we hiave a telegraph line that will connect that part of our system with the prospective Australian cable. The time may not he distant when, our telegraph system in the Yukon may be connected with advantage with that cable. I think we should make ourselves as much at home a,s possible on land and sea. Regarding the matter from that standpoint, I take the liberty of calling the attention of the House to the maps of our country, asking hon. members to study them. These are not party questions, and I think a more careful study of the map would help us to solve many difficulties to the advantage of the country.

Speaking with some experience in this business, I would suggest that the government is much more likely to make -money by lowering the rates than by keeping them at high figures. They have their staff, which they must keep in working order, and they must keep the batteries and supply the electricity. The outfit is there, and the men are there, and might as well be employed. I understand that a message costs about $5.
lit is $4.50 between Dawson city and Ashcroft.

At that rate, if a mail can wait for a letter he is not going to telegraph. But, by lowering the rates, you will induce him ,to send two, or even three, messages where be would send only one. The expenses are about the same, whether we send ten messages or ten thousand. The men on the staff would just as soon be employed. If you keep operators employed steadily as some of the men here are kept during the whole working day, passing messages through their hands .ait the rate of one a minute, a comparatively low rate will make money for the line. But, with High rates, the men will sit with their heels on window sills. From practical experience, I would say :	Lower the rates. Moreover, whenever the government is prepared to take over the whole telegraph system of the country, they will have my support; for I believe we could have our telegraphing done a igreat deal cheaper than we have now. I have said before, and I say again, we ought to have our telegraphing done for a cent a word anywhere within reasonable distances in Canada.

I have made the press rates on the Yukon line one cent a word. Tihe rate was three cents a word, but I (Changed that, for, at these rates, the newspaper men could not use our line. Since then, we have made pretty good business. The trouble is. if I

lower the nates and the result is not favourable, it will be difficult to raise them again. I am sure there is a gooid deal in the suggestion that has been made. When the session is over, I intend to give my best consideration to the rates on our telegraph lines in general. And when the (supplementary estimates come up for discussion, I hope we shall discuss the subject at greater length. There are good opportunities now to make ourselves independent in these matters. Our telegraph system has been completed to Belle Isle, and now it is finished to Murray Bay. It would take very little to complete it and carry it up to the city of Montreal; and instead of relying on New York for our coronation news, we may make Montreal a distributing centre for the news. From the British standpoint and from the Canadian standpoint it would 'be better.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I fully eudorse the sentiment expressed by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd). I think the rates we are paying for telegraphing in this country are rather too high, much higher than in cases where lines are owned by the government. I hope to see the day when the whole telegraph system of the Dominion of Canada will be under the control of the government. I am glad to find that that sentiment is increasing rapidly on both sides of the House. Look at our condition to-day. We are laying a telegraxoh cable between our own country and Australia and New Zealand, and the moment you land in British Columbia you are at the mercy of a telegraph company. Then when you come to the Atlantic you are at the mercy of another telegraph company. All the lines from Australia to Great Britain and to the continent should be owned by the government. I hope when our friends go over to London to discuss all these large questions among the representatives of the different colonies, this question will come under their consideration.
I would like on another occasion if the minister would give us the average number of words that have been sent daily since the line was opened, on the average number of messages.
I would suggest to the minister that he should take action during this busy season of the year, and if he is going to make any change in prices, it should be made early.
I will discuss the question to-night. But I must warn the hon. gentlemen that if 1 find I am losing too much, I will raise the rates again.
I am satisfied he will make more money by lowering the rates to a figure where the line can be generally used.
The minister can readily ascertain from experts what the capacity of the line is. There are certain fixed charges that must be borne.

The line is all right. From what I can learn, we can do a much larger business. It is a question whether we are receiving all the business that is to be had at the rates we are now charging. I have often discussed the matter with my officers, and they do not share the views that I have expressed here. I have been advised by them that it would not be wise to decrease the rates. But having reduced the expenditure I think we may fairly try to reduce the rates a little.
I understand the minister is going to make a comprehensive statement on some other item of his policy respecting telegraph lines, and telephones as well.
I have not much to do with telephones. I am not the minister of telephones, and I do not know who is. I cannot find the minister of telephones, so far.

We will limit it to telegraphs, then.
Telegraphs - Port Simpson - Hazel tori telegraph line, $25,100.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC 'WORKS. This is practically the same. We require more to complete from Port Simpson, because, instead of the line being 130 miles long, as we expected, we find it is 200 miles long.
Why did the hon. gentleman not have this $107,000 for the Quesnel-Atlin telegraph line in the main estimates last year ?

We had not sufficient information, the country had never been explored.
New Brunswick-St. John imjnigrant building, including interest to contractor on overdue amounts, $12,000.
Wby do you want this ?
To carry out the work on the immigration building at St. John. The total cost of the work is estimated to be $33,596.
Why is there interest on overdue accounts ? Were the contractors not paid ?
We had not enough money to pay the contractor, and we are obliged to pay interest on what we are owing him.
Why did you not have enough money ?
Because we did not ask for enough. The contractor went faster than I thought he was going. We are paying 5 per cent interest.
Was there any competition for tenders for this building ?

Yes, there were public tenders and the lowest was accepted.
Quebec-Peribonka-immigrant building, $1,500.
This is in the Lake St. John district. A large number of immigrants are settling there, coming from Holland, Belgium, Finland and all parts of the continent.
In what part of the province is it ?
In the Lake St. John district. I would invite the hon. gentleman to visit that place. We will give you the freedom of the country.

Will the hon. gentleman take me in as an immigrant ?
The MINIS-lER OF PUBLIC WORKS. If the hon. gentleman went there I think he would settle.
I thought the object was to bring Canadians back from the United States and induce them to settle in that district ?

No. There are' some Canadians from the United States and the North-west Territories, but this is purely immigration from abroad. This season on one train, there were 700 people who came from the continent. Large numbers of settlers are going in and they are of a good class. I am informed by the Colonization Company of Quebec that these people have enough money to buy property, and settle in a comfortable way.
Were the agents of this government or the local government instrumental in getting people to go to that district ?

There is in the city of Quebec a colonization company which is a kind of independent company working with the corporation of the Lake St. John Railway Company. Mr. Dupont went last year to the continent of Europe, and I understand he has been very successful indeed. The local government have helped and this government have helped the railway company by giving them $8,000 a year during the last five or six years.
This is to complete the building.

Yes.
Roberval, immigration building, $2,650.
The very same object.
Does that complete the building ?

Yes.
St. Jerome public building-improvements, repairs, &c., $1,775.
What is the meaning of this ?

These are small repairs to the public building which is in existence at St. Jerome in the county of Terrebonne behind Montreal.
Quebec Military buildings-rolling mill for cartridge factory, $2,000.
This is to complete the work that is under contract.
Rolling mill or cartridge factory ?

Yes, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) knows, the Department of Militia and Defence manufacture arms In Quebec, and I am the builder for the department.
Drummondville public buildings, $2,000.
To complete.
How much is the total cost ?
By contract ?
Yes, by contract and by public tender.
Why did you not have it in last year's estimates ?

We were short. We give contracts for public buildings and when we come to pay for them we find we are short.
Ottawa-Majors Hill park, plant house, &c.,
Would the hon. gentleman kindly explain this ?

During last session of parliament the House gave me a sum of money-$8,000-if I remember rightly-less than that, for greenhouses in Major's Hill park. When we were about to arrange for the work Sir Sanford Fleming made us a gift of a very valuable collection of plants. Then I thought mat while we were at work it would be just as well to have a green house of larger dimen-

sions than the one we contemplated at first,
I took it upon myself, X may say, to change the plans that had been entertained and to build a more expensive green house. I think Major's Hill park is an ornament to the House and it is a portion of the government grounds. Although we have not decided altogether on the site, we contemplate the idea of erecting our museum on the Major's Hill park ground. A few thousand dollars more or less under circumstances of than kind. X think, do not amount to much. I am asking the indulgence of the House for the change which I have taken upon myself to make.
I think that these park grounds should he made as nice as we can make them without spending too much money. I am sorry to say that under the system of contract which has been in existence for some years the grounds have been allowed to run down too much. I have changed the system. I have given charge of the grounds here and of Major's Hill park to Mr. Davis who is a very capable man. For these reasons I am asking the House for this amount of money.

Is this a new building ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WOKivS. Yes, it is not yet painted, but I think it is all right.
What is me total cost ?
About $14,000 to complete ; including the heating and fittings. Part of the work has been done by contract by the W. C. Edwards Company.
What is the use of it particularly ?

Of course, it is to winter our plants. We must have plant houses aud greenhouses to winter the plants that we use on the ground here and at the same time it beautifies the city and the government property.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman erected this building before he came to parliament and asked for a grant with which to build it. I passed there the other day and I found it completed. I inquired what it was and they said it was a new building that the government had erected.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WoBivci. I had a grant last year.
Mr. TAYeoR. To erect this building ?

Yes, to erect this building, but when I changed the plans I found that I required more.
Dominion public buildings-improvements, repairs, &c., $2,000.
What is the reason for this increase ?

This is not an increase. My hon friend must not lose sight of the fact that the number of our public buildings is increasing. Many of them are run down and they are in very bad shape. We want this money for small repairs.
These are all over Ontario ?

Yes.
Brockville drill hall, $2,500.
To pay the balance of the contract.
How much was the total contract ?

The contract was for $42,000, the worn having been awarded to the lowest tenderer.
Toronto Post Office-building for branch office in west end of city, site, &c., $15,000.
What will the new building cost in the west end ?
It will cost, we expect, about $35,000.
Yes.
How much of it will be for the site ?
$6,000 for the site.
From whom was the site purchased ?
From the Land Security Company.
Is it the intention of tne government to improve the old post office ? There is nothing in the estimates.

No, but if my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) allows me, when the supplementary estimates come down he will find, I hope, that we will have some money to improve the old building. Our intention at first was to enlarge the old building, but the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) has made up his mind to have a new system. He thinks that sub-stations will give a better service. When tne mail is delivered at the main post office in Toronto it takes a good deal of time to denver newspapers and letters, but in future they will be delivered direct to the sub-stations and the distribution will be quicker.

We had quite a discussion on this point the other evening. Hon. members speaking on behalf of Winnipeg, Montreal. Charlottetown and Toronto, questioned the Postmaster General in regard to these matters. It appears that Montreal is also i*

a bad position regarding post office facilities as well as Toronto. This question of subpost offices is an important matter for the Minister of Public Works to consider. It is departing altogether from the principle that has been adopted in all large cities on this continent and In other places. It would be a great credit to the city of Toronto and to the country, if we had one first-class post office building in that city, and I suppose the same would apply to Montreal. For my part I do not think the policy of sub-offices is a wise one. If these branch post offices have to be erected at a considerable expense, that principle will involve the doing away with the central building to some extent. If the present post office in Toronto is not suitable, then a first class building should be erected. The responsibility does not rest altogether on the shoulders of the Postmaster General because the Minister of Public Works has charge of the public buildings, and he ought to have something to say on the matter. If the present post office in Toronto is not in the centre of the business part of the city, then the government could dispose of that property to advantage and erect a first class building in the centre of the city. This principle of doing away with a central building is a radical change, and I would like to hear the views of the Minister of Public Works in respect to it.

On questions of policy of this kind the Minister of Public Works is only responsible as one member of the government. When my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) is Postmaster General, some time in the future, he will make recommendations to his colleagues and they will accept them or not. In the present case it is evident that the Government in Council have agreed to erect sub-stations, and I become a builder pure and simple, carrying out the instructions of my colleagues. The government have decided on the recommendation of the Postmaster General to adopt the sub-station policy, and I am charged with the duty of erecting buildings not only for the Postmaster General but for all my colleagues. As to the wisdom of such a policy, I think my kon. friend, on reflection, will agree that there is a good deal in it. Toronto and Montreal are becoming large centres of population and the people want rapid distribution of the mails. In Montreal a letter which reaches the post office in the morning is often not delivered at my house until 11 o'clock. The Postmaster General thinks that by subdividing the work he will get better service all around.
In what other place in the world is this system in existence ?
I have enough of my own work to defend without having to defend the Postmaster General. On this occasion I am prepared to defend the erection of this building. ' Mr. KEMP.

This matter was brought to the attention of the House a few days ago when the Postmaster General was present. The difficulty in Toronto is that the main post office is now in the wrong part of the city. Toronto has made substantial progress westward, has annexed some municipalities in that direction, and the great bulk of the population is now far west of the general post office. We believe that what is the more pressing necessity is the construction of a main post office building further west and north of the present site, which is not even on the line of the tram cars.
The post office in New York is very far from the centre of population, and sub-stations are in existence there.

In view of the opinion expressed by the Postmaster General, I speak with a good deal of diffidence, but I think it will be found that his idea will not facilitate distribution. ,The erection of a main post office building within easy access of the Union railway station and on the line of the tram cars is what we want to give us a more rapid service.
Alexandria Reformatory-balance of arbitration, $174.02.
Why is it that we have so many of these small votes to complete contracts which are supposed to be let by tender?

The policy of the department has been to vote only the money that we expect to spend during the year, and then afterwards we ask for the balance. Suppose I am erecting a building in Halifax which will cost say $200,000, I ask for only $20,000 or $30,000 which I will expect to expend during the current year.

But these contracts usually provide that the work shall be completed within a fixed time, and it seems to me it would not be a very difficult matter to provide for an adequate vote each year without bringing in all these supplementary estimates and dividing it up so that one cannot get an adequate idea as to what the whole work will cost.
It is very difficult to make an accurate estimate.
The trouble is that in all these contracts the cost is far in excess of the original estimate.
Oh, no.
What was the original tender for the Broekville drill hall ?
My hon. friend must not lose sight of the
fact that in addition to the contract there are the fittings, the heating, and so forth.
What was the original estimate, and what is the amount of the contract ?

My officers tell me that their estimate was $55,000 for the whole work, heating and all, and it will be completed for that amount. The estimate for the building was $42,200. The amount of the contract is $42,000, and there are no extras.
Is this Alexandria reformatory built ?
No.
What did it cost to get rid of the obligation ?
I do not remember; a small amount of money.
Then, it is not the intention of the government to have a reformatory for boys ?
Not there.
Then, it takes $13,000 to fit up the interior of the drill hall in Brockville ?

Heating, fitting, sidewalks, footpath, and things of that kind.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock. Lethbridge immigration building, $2,600.

This work is under contract. The total cost will be $5,600. This will complete it.
Kamloops public building, $2,000.

This work is under contract. This vote is to complete It. The total cost is $20,000.
New Westminster public building-reconstruction, $8,000.
The original building was burned down. This work is under contract, and this vote will complete it.
Has there been no public building in New Westminster since the time of the fire there some years ago ?
We have rented one.
What is the total cost of this ?
Vancouver drill hall, $7,000.
What is the total cost of the work ?
$100,000. I understand that the cost of the site was given free of cost by the provincial government.
I suppose all these 'buildings were constructed by public tender ?

Yes
Public buildings generally, $2,000.
Why is there a general item of this kind in the supplementary estimates ?

We have so many public buildings, it is ouit of the question to see in advance what small repairs are required. The caretaker writes to the chief architect thiat such and such repairs are required, and we have to provide for them.
Salaries of resident clerks of works, assistants, $2,800.
I can see no reason why this should not have been in the main estimates ?
We were short on this appropriation because we have more work than we ever had, and it is necessary to have more officers.
How many more officers have you employed since this time last year on these buildings ?
It is pretty hard to have all these details at a moments notice. Some day when my hon. friends are in my place and I am in theirs, they will appreciate the difficulty.
Are these resident clerks of works men who are temporarily employed ?

No, they are officers who have charge of certain districts. In Quebec we have Mr. Belland; in St. An,nes, we have Mr. Water-bury; in Halifax, we have Mr. Doddbum; in the North-west Territories, -we have Mr. Paradis ; and in British Columbia, Mr. Henderson.
That does not cover Mr. Henderson's salary ?

No, travelling expenses, and so on.
Toronto Post Office locomobiles-maintenance of, $5,000.

We want a very elaborate statement from the minister about these

locomobiles. I have seen them in all stages of decrepitude on the streets of Toronto. One-third of their time was spent in the blacksmith shop, and the unfortunate postmen who were obliged to use them had to spend part of their time in the hospital. They have proved a dismal failure. The hen. minister is not responsible for the purchase of these machines, because the purchase was recommended by the Postmaster General, but we ought to know what they cost in the first plaice, then how much it has cost to maintain them, and how much time has been lost by the employees who attempted to utilize them. I hope the hon. minister, ill view of his expensive experience, will abandon these machines on- pass them over to the Post Office Department.
What is a locomobile 1
It is a machine which is one-third oif the time on the road, one-third in the ditch, and one-third in the repair shop.

While I was representing to the best of my ability, my country in a foreign land, my progressive and economical colleague, the Postmaster General, unloaded those locomobiles on my department. I have to carry the load and to give the best information my limited ability will permit. Those locomobiles do not seem to have given the satisfaction which the Postmaster General expected from them, and I am not going to ask anything for their maintenance in my estimates for next year, but this year I have to foot the bill. The Postmaster General tried the experiment and we have to pay for it. I do not know anything more about the matter except that as the service did not turn out very satisfactory, we are going to put an end to the employment of these machines in Toronto.
How many did you buy ?
My department has nine.
If the hon. gentleman would get them repaired, he might take them over to England and challenge the Australia nis to a race between London and Brighton.
I think that His Majesty can be crowned without those.

Before the locomobiles came into use, the mails were gathered by officials using horses and wagons. After these machines go out of use, will the hon. minister have charge of the carriages and horses ?

I hope not. I have had enough of the locomobiles. They were unloaded on me while I was away, and the Postmaster Gen-Mr. CLARKE.
eral will have to answer for any expense he may incur in the future.
How much did they cost ?
They cost 81,000 each. It was an experiment. It is true, it has not succeeded very well.

Why does the Minister of Public Works allow the Postmaster General to experiment in this way at his expense 1 The policy in regard to the post office "building in Toronto is the policy of the Postmaster General, but the Minister of Public Works does not approve of it. Here is another policy which the Postmaster General has forced on the Minister of Public Works Why does he sanction it ?

Well, in his absence, the Minister of Public Works appoints, as master of the administration for the time being, the Postmaster General. The Postmaster General wants to be economical and at the same time to make improvements. So he unloads his experiments upon me.
Then the Minister of Public Works has to father these schemes ?

Let the hon. gentlemen wait until the Postmaster General is in his seat, and then he will answer them all.
Riideau Hall, including grounds - Improvements, renewals and maintenance, $7,500.
What was the total spent on Rideau Hall ?

We have spent a large sum of money ou Rideau Hall, but largely to fit it for the reception of their Royal Highnesses on their recent visit. I venture to say that the Vice Regal buildings are in better condition today than they have ever been in the past.
Are the expenses of this service any more than they were under the Conservative regime ?

There were years when the Conservatives spent less. During the last year or two of the Conservative regime, when Mr. Poster was Minister of Finance, they did not spend so much on Rideau Hall. But then their party was killed-killed outright.

I do not wish to complain about the expenditure on Rideau Hall. But, when hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side of the House, one of their number used to relive in finding fault with this expenditure. I merely wished to know if the expenditure had grown less.

No. A couple of years ago I gave a statement of the expenditures on Rideau Hall.

Under Lord Dufferin the expenditure was never less than $30,000 a year. Under other Governors General we have spent a little less. The expenditure, I think, is wisely made.
I am not finding fault with it ; but, as fault has been found with the expenditure under the Conservatives, I wished to know the facts.
One thing I would like to know is this-if everything about Rideau Hall is in such fine condition, whv does the hon. gentleman want this $7,500 ?

To pay for putting it in such fine condition.
Lighting Dominion public buildings, $18,000.

The appropriation has been the same for a good many years, but, for the last two or three years we have had a deficit of $3,000 or $4,000 a year. We have more public buildings, as hon. gentlemen know, and we must, of course, spend more money. These accounts are paid just as they are sent to us. This question of lighting is supervised by the department. It is a work that cannot be curtailed.
Ottawa public buildings-heating, including salaries of engineers, firemen, elevator attendants and caretaker, $12,000.
I have just explained how this item arises, we are obliged to ask for more because we have more public buildings.
I thought the hon. minister had an item this afternoon that covered this ?

I said this afternoon that it would be necessary for me to ask for $24,000 because we spent $15,000 additional for the purchase of coal alone.
Ottawa public buildings-gas and electric light including light for roads and bridges, $7,300.
As my hon. friends know, we have installed a new electric lighting system. We have more public buildings to provide for under this item and the expense is greater.
How is the lighting done, by tender ?

We have a contract. This covers the cost of gas also, which is used in some of the departments, including the Inland Revenue and the Museum. The main reason for this increase is the installation of an electric light system for the Senate, the same as we have for this chamber.
Is the light paid for by meter ?

No. It is a flat rate-two dollars per light per year.
Public Works-chargeable to income-public buildings-Yukon Territory-rents, beating, inclusive of fuel, lighting, water service, scavenging, janitors, watchmen, repairs, &c., $48,000.

I have already explained this item on the main estimate. It is the last year I am to ask the House to give my department any appropriation for this purpose. As I have said, these items will be transferred to the Yukon government with the exception of the federal buildings, that is the post office, the administration building and the residence of the Governor.
Who supervises the expenditure of this money 1
Up to a few weeks ago, our resident architect was Mr. Fuller, and he had full charge of that expenditure, under Mr. Ross, commissioner of the Yukon.
What rents do you pay in addition to the four buildings mentioned this afternoon ?

The rents include the following. Gold Commissioner's residence ; residence for Judge Dugas ; residence for Judge Craig ; mining inspector's office ; Silver Creek ; mining inspector's office, Gold Run ; mining inspector's office, Stewart River ; mining inspector's office, Dominion Creek ; mining inspector's office, Hunker.
What is the total amount of rents ?
The total Is $4,267.
These judges have an allowance of $5,000 In addition to their salary. Do we also provide them with house rent ?
So far, we have paid their rent.
How much do we allow for rent in addition to the $5,000 expenses ?
Judge Dugas, $150 a month ; Judge Craig, the same.
As I understood it, then each judge gets his salary, $5,000 living expenses and $1,800 for rent. That is, he gets $6,800 as a living allowance.

Yes, the Department of Justice has control of this whole matter, and I only obey orders. When the Governor General in Council decides that a judge must be lodged and housed, they simply notify me, and I have to make provision.
In addition to that, there is the heating. Does the government pay for the heating of Judge Dugas' house ?
When the main estimates were discussed, I gave a complete statement, covering a page of foolscap, giving all these details.
The minister must know whether the judges get their heating.
I gave the information a month ago, but I do not remember it now. I am informed that they get fuel, I do not know the amount per annum. It depends upon the price of firewood.
Then there is the lighting.
They get that also.
And water service ?
I suppose so, yes.
And men to attend to their houses ?
No.
Then, according to that, a judge in the Yukon gets a salary of $5,000, $5,000 living expenses, $1,800 a year for rent, and his heating, fuel and water service ?
Yes, and the judges are complaining very bitterly, indeed.
He gets about $14,000 or $15,000 a year. The Minister of Justice shouid explain that, let ns understand it thoroughly.
Under the law, he is entitled to $5,000 a year for his salary at the present time and $3,000 a year for living allowance. I am telling what the law is.' I have nothing to say further than that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: I think the Minister of Justice stated the other night that that is to be changed.
I am telling you now what the law is, and I will tell you by-and-by what the law will be.
If you will explain it now it wnl save the trouble of explaining it hereafter.
I am telling you what the law is. Next year, by virtue of a statute passed here, the judges will have $5,000 a year salary and $5,000 a year living expenses.
That comes right back to the point I stated. It was stated in this House that a judge in the Yukon would have $5,000 a year living expenses.
That is what he will have next year after the 1st of July. What he is getting now is $3,000.
We are just now dealing with the supplementary estimates for the coming year, when we will have to pay $5,000 a year for living allowances.
This coming year is the $5,000 to include the rental ?
If the Minister of Justice tells me to pay rents I shall do so. But he has just said that for the next year the judges will have $5,000 a year for living allowance.

I think it is only fair that we should know whether the $5,000 includes rental. The Minister of Justice should state whether, out of that $5,000, the judge is to pay his own rental, lighting, fuel and living expenses.

Some days ago we had all this up in the House, we discussed the whole subject here, and when the question arose as to the additional allowance to be given to the judges next year, and I was asked how it was intended this amount should be spent, I then went over the list I had, showing how much would go for rent, how much for lighting, how much for fuel, and I gave all the details to the House to justify the increase.
I do not remember that this particular fact was mentioned by the Minister of Justice.
I read from a list provided by the commissioner of tire Yukon, showing the amounts to be expended, so as to justify the increase from $3,000 to $5,000.
The rental was mentioned, was it ?
Yes, $150 a month. I mentioned the wood and the lighting.
What we are anxious to get at now is whether the $5,000 he is to be paid covers every one of these items the Minister of Justice has mentioned.
That certainly was the intention at the time the item was put in the estimates, that $5,000 would cover everything, and we would have no more of these outside claims. That is the intention now.
I did not understand it as the Minister of Justice has explained it now, and I think I was quite */ justified in getting it fairly understood.
Of course you were.
(Translation.) Who hires those people '!
(Translation.) It is the department which hired them.
(Translation.) By whom are they paid ?
(Translation.) So far, we have paid them ourselves.
(Translation.) Under whose control are they ?

(Translation.) They are under the control of the resident architect, Mr. Fuller, who is here now. As I have said before, all public buildings used for what may be called provincial purposes, will be handed over to the Yukon government in the future, and only the Dominion buildings will remain under our control, such as the government house, if it may be so called, and the post office. As to all the other provincial buildings, they will be transferred to the Yukon government, because they are used for local purposes.
(Translation.) Has the Department of Public Works notified Mrs. Louise Collinet that her usefulness was gone ?

(Translation.) We have nothing to do with that staff.
That is quite another story. We pay the sheriff and the caretakers, but those officials are not under our control. Mrs. Collinet is the matron of the court-house. There are a certain number of employees who are under the control of the Department of Justice, with whom I have nothing to do. I have no doubt but that Mrs. Collinet belongs to that class of employees, and I may say that I know nothing about her.
(Translation.) To whom was it written ?

(Translation.) To the Deputy Minister of Justice. When Mrs.
1 Louise Collinet was engaged by tbe depart-



ment a man named Willie St. Denis was also hired at the same time. Both have been discharged on the same grounds, and on the 1st April, 1902, Willie St. Denis wrote to the Deputy Minister of Justice, as follows :

, April 1, 1902.
To the Deputy Minister of Justice,
Ottawa, Canada.
Sir,-On September 6,1899, I began service as caretaker of the court house, and man-servant for Mr. Justice Dugas. On the 21st day of March, 1902, I was discharged from my dual position without cause. I ask to be reinstated in my position or some reason given for my discharge. I wish my appointment made from Ottawa and my duties defined, as for the period of my service my chief duties were as manservant in the judge's private residence, and out of the $160 per month allowed me for my services, I was forced to repay $40 per month to said Mr. Justice Dugas. Said Mr. Justice Dugas d'seharged me because I refused to act as ebamberman in his house, wait on his tables, prepare wood, draw water and do general cleaning work in his residence in addition to my duties as caretaker of said court house. I wish to know whether such were a part of my duties and whether said judge had a right to force me to repay his said $40 per month.
Yours respectfully,
(Sgd.) WILLIE ST. DENNIS. On the 12th April he wrote again, as follows :
Dawson, Y.T.. April 12, 1902. To the Deputy Minister of Public Works, Ottawa, Canada.
Sir,-On April 1, 1902, I addressed a letter to the Deputy Minister of Justice, which letter ere this must have reached his destination. In that I complain of my wrongful discharge from the position of caretaker of the court house here, and persecution hy Mr. Justice Dugas.
I after being discharged, obtain the position as n'ght watchman in the post office, and gave first-class satisfaction in that position, as has been testified to by the postmaster, Mr. Hartman, and Mr. Bertrand of the Department of Public Works here.
I was on the 11th day of April, 1902. discharged from this latter position, without cause, and was to-day informed by Mr. Bertrand that he has been forced to discharge mo hy Judge Dugas who dislikes me, and insisted that a nephew of J. E. Girouard, Jean Marier, who arrived in Dawson Monday last, be appointed in my stead.
I ask to be reinstated in one or the other of my potations, and believe I had a right to the first, from which I was driven by the persecution of Mr. Justice Dugas.
Yours respectfully,

Now, I should like to know front the hon. Minister of Public Works, whether these two persons, employed as caretakers of the court-house at Dawson City, are under the immediate control of the Minister of Public Works ?
Heretofore the caretakers have been under our charge, but in the future they will not

be under our charge. I cannot, of course, say anything as to the people to whom my hon. friend (Mr. Leonard) has just alluded.
I do not know anything about their case. The letters are all of recent date, and I have not read them. This is the first 1 have heard of them. I cannot believe that a judge could be repaid by people of that class. Of course, Iedo not know anything about it. It is all new to me. I will inquire into the case. I will write to Mr. Bertrand and ask: for an explanation in regard to these people. But, until I hear more 1 cannot have any faith in charges of that kind. People who are dismissed are generally not in a very good humour. In fact, I do not know anything about the case. The hon. -Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) is within reach of the voice of my hon. friend (Mr. Leonard), and surely, if a judge would be guilty of such a thing it would be very extraordinary.

The hon. minister should at least know whether or not such an order was issued as purports to have been Issued, dated 1st July, 1901, from the resident architect of his department to this woman Louise Collinet:
Dawson, Y. T., July 1, 1901. Louise Collinet, Matron,
Court House,
Dawson, Y.T.
MJadam,-Rations having been withdrawn from you, it has been decided to allow you therefor $30 per month, which you will receive in addition to your wages of $80 per mouth. You will continue therefore to be at .he service of Mr. Justice Dugas and act under his guidance for any work which you will be required to do as matron of the court house.
Who writes such an order ?
T. W. Fuller, resident architect of the Department of Public Works.	.
Mr. Fuller is here now.

Quite so. The letter continues as follows :
You will arrange with the judge for your meals, which, under any circumstances, must not be taken within the court house. No fire is to be made therein for the purpose of cooking, &c., nor arc strangers to be received there by you, unless specially authorized.
(Sgd.) T. W. FULLER, Resident Architect, Department of Public Works.
It would be desirable, so far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, to know why the matron of the court house should be at the service of Mr. Justice Dugas and to act under his guidance for any work which she should be required to do as matron of the court house. It should he a matter f< r the hon. Minister of Justice to investigate why the matron of the court

house should be at the service of Mr. Justice Dugas and under his guidance in any work which she shall be required to do.
I cannot understand it.

It is something that the hon. minister will have to understand and the committee will have to understand. I would like to ask the lion. Minister of Justice as to whether or not such a letter has been received in his department as that which has been read by my hon. friend (Mr. Leonard) ?

Such a letter was received at the Department of Justice and immediately forwarded to the Department of Public Works, as we had absolutely no control over this lady who calls herself the matron of the court house not having anything to do with her appointment.

The secretary of my department, who is on the floor now, says that he received these documents to-day. I did not know anything about them until they were read on the floor of the House now. I will inquire of Mr. Fuller to-morrow and ascertain what he has done in the matter. I cannot understand it.
These statements are of a very extraordinary nature.
They are very extraordinary.
And I think the item should stand until the hon. gentleman is able to explain them.
There is no reason why the item should stand. I have promised to bring down the information to-morrow. Let us go on with the work.
We can take up some other item if necessary, but we must have an explanation of the matter.
1 shall bring the information to-morrow.

This woman alleges-I do not know with what truth- that while she was ostensibly acting as matron of the court house she was really a servant in the private residence of Mr. Justice Dugas. Further than that she states, what I can hardly believe to be true and what I would certainly very greatly regret to believe to be true, that of her allowance of $110 a month she was forced to repay a portion.
I cannot understand that.

Letters which have been received in the Department of Public Works certainly call for some in-132*
quiry. I should think not only would they require an inquiry by the Department of Public Works but also by the Department of Justice, although the hon. Minister of Justice has sent the whole of the correspondence to the hon. Minister of Public Works.
It would seem to me a very improper thing that any such transaction should have taken place, and I am not disposed to believe for the present that it did take place, but there is the statement of this man Willie St. Denis that he has repaid a portion of his allowance to an official occupying a judicial position. So far as that is concerned it ought to have some inquiry, not only from the Department of Public Works, but the Department of Justice as well.

I willl wire immediately to Mr. Justice Dugas and the employee he is accused by of having received a commission, because it amounts to that. I will wire the contents of the letter and in the morning I will call Mr. Fuller in and lay the matter before him.
Would the judge be violating his position if he collected tolls from an employee of that kind ?

There is no use asking that. It is a clear case if it is true, but I cannot believe it.
It has no sense.

Of course I know nothing about this. I was always under the impression, and still am under the impression, that when a judge gets $5,000 a year of salary and in addition to that $3,000 a year for living allowance, he ought to apply that living allowance to the reasonable charges of his household, and payment for all these things which men require for living should be paid out of the $3,000. With respect to this woman who made the complaint I understand the facts to be that she went up there as a matron, and as an employee of the government originally she would have been entitled to rations, but that living with the judge the rations went in the common fund. She was boarded [DOT] by the judge and the rations used by the judge for the purpose of her maintenance as well. I understand there is nothing beyond that. If that is what really took place it is not a serious matter, but when you go beyond that and extend it to say that instead of rations she received $40 a month for her living allowance and that this $40 a month was paid over to the judge-well, if she lived with the judge and it was a matter of bargain between them, that they would put their allowance into a common fund there was nothing very wrong about that either. But if the judge received the money and did not'supply this woman with her board, of course that is a matter that ought be investigated, and so far as I am concerned, he is going to hear about it if it is a fact.	.
Mr. Fuller will have to tell us to-morrow what are the facts of the ease, and if I have the information before the orders of the day are called to-morrow I will give it with pleasure.

I would not tfiink it was a desirable thing this matron drawing rations should live with the judge, and that the judge should draw the rations instead of her. I would not consider that a desirable position for a gentleman occupying a seat on the Supreme Court of the Yukon, even if it did not go beyond that. I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice would regard it as a very desirable condition of affairs either.
They must be living under very abnormal conditions in that country.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice puts it very mildly to say the least when he says that. As the hon. gentleman very truly remarks, there is something beyond that in the statement, not only of this woman, but the man as well, who says he was performing the duties of manservant for Mr. Justice Dugas, and that he was making an allowance to that gentleman out of the amount which he received. I will not ask that i the item should stand on this account, because I appreciate the reasons which influence the Minister of Public Works, but it must be distinctly understood that at some future occasion we shall have an opportunity of obtaining information and discussing it.

If I have the information I will bring it down to-morrow morning.
of the Auditor General I find that we have spent $4,128.67 for fitting up a residence for Mr. Justice Dugas. What arrangement is to be made about that residence in the future ?
The Department of Public Works has been guided in this matter by the Department of Justice. When we are asked to supply a judge's residence with light or anything of that kind we do it.
Does this building belong to the Department of Public Works?
We have rented it.
You pay for fitting it up and pay rent as well ?
Well, it often happens, even in the city of Ottawa, that we ha\% to repair buildings that we pay rent on. We will pay no more rentals in the Yukon after the 1st of July.

Judge Dugas received $5,000 as salary last year and $4,128 was paid for his rent and for fitting up his house. Judge Dugas has his house this year complete, so that actually he is getting an increase of $2,300 on his salary.
We have paid the amount as the hon. gentleman says, but there will not be such an expenditure after this year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Who contracted the debts ? Who authorized the payments ?
I am not in a position to give more information, I am sorry to say.

The hon. Minister of Justice could explain that item. Two nights ago he stated that Judge Dugas was to receive last year $5,000 salary and $3,000 foir living expenses, whereas $4,128 in addition was spent on these various items for living expenses.

Last year, so far as my information goes, and so far as the law goes, Judge Dugas was entitled to receive for his salary $5,000 and for his living allowance $3,000, and for next year he is entitled to receive $5,000 for his salary and $5,000 for living allowance. Of any expenses beyond that I know nothing whatever.
And for next year I shall not pay one dollar.

So far as my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is concerned, he has assumed charge of his department only recently. We are not attacking the Minister of Justice. We are making our charge upon the government. It is a mere accident, so far as we are concerned, that one minister goes out and another comes in.
(Translation.) Would the hon. minister also inquire on what grounds Judge Dugas discharged from his service a person hired by the month, without giving that person a day's notice ?
(Translation.) I know nothing about that case. I cannot understand it.

(Translation.) At all events, as a member of this House, I lay before the House the fact that those employees made an allowance to Judge Dugas, out of the amount which they received, to be retained in his service. The Minister of Justice told us that those sums were paid over to the judge by those employees because they were boarded by the judge. But I should like to know since when a manservant or a maid-servant have to pay their master, to be retained in his service ? On the contrary, it is the master who pays the servants.

I understand that in future the judge has to provide his own residence and is to receive an allowance of $5,000 for living expenses. In the report Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.

The Department of Justice is not responsible for this. It is not money expended by us at all.

I thoroughly appreciate that; but it is money expended in connection with the administration of justice in this country, over which the de-[DOT] partment of my hon. friend presides. Last year this gentleman got $5,000 of salary and $3,000 of living allowance, and this sum of $4,128.67 was expended for him in addition, of which I think $900 was for rental. If you deduct $900 from $4,12S.G7, you have $3,228.67 expended on this rented house.

No, no. We have spent $990 for fuel, $776 for lighting, and $1,800 for rent. In past days the policy of the Department of Justice was that we should pay these items in the Yukon, and I paid them. Outside of these, the expenditure is very small.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is the $3,000 living allowance for ?

It is not for me to say. We have simply been instructed to pay for the rent, the fuel and the lighting, and we have done so. It will not happen again. There is not much pleasure in the poor Minister of Public Works being sacrificed because he carries out the orders of the other departments.

I am as sorry as I can be for the Minister of rublic Works, and I think some of the other ministers should take a turn when any of these items prove too much for him. Let me run over same of these expenditures again. We have the Dawson Electric & Power Company, for installing 16 lights, 2 four-light fixtures, 1 two-light fixture, 2 brackets combined, into one, and 1 stand lamp $152.75 ; lighting, from October to April : 13 lamps, 192 nights, and 4 lamps, 173 nights, $776 ; F. A. Delage, repairs, $535.70; D. A. Matheson, 45 cords of firewood, $990 ; McLennan, McFeely & Company, sundry repairs $340.15; P. G. Overton, painting, $41.20; Cortland, Starnes, rent $900; Yukon Saw Mill Company, lumber, $339.87; amounting in all to $4,128.67. What I want to know is under what rental agreement is this house held from Mr. Starnes ?
No man could carry all these details. I understand that we have paid $150 a month for the house since the judge occupied it.
I cannot say more than I have said. The amounts have been paid, and I do not See a way of getting them 'back.
I see a way of getting them back. If Judge Dugas was paid $3,000 for living allowance, and it was intended to include all these items, he should refund the money. I do not think that is unreasonable.

I have only paid what I was instructed to pay and nothing- more. If the Department of Justice wishes to inquire into this matter, it can do so.
Mi-. BORDEN (Halifax). Mr. Justice Dugas has been paid $3,000 for living expenses. Besides these the Department of Public Works has paid $990 for his heating, $928.75 for his lighting and installing his lights, and $1,309.92 for repairing his house, in addition to $1,800 for his rent. If his living expenses mean anything, surely they must include his heating and lighting. The Minister of Public Works tells us that he has paid these moneys by the instructions of some person. What department or person 1

I have just said that the Minister of Justice instructed me to pay the rent for the judge's residence and fuel and light. We did that in the past. Things were in great confusion for a year or two-not much order anywhere. There were no funds available elsewhere, and we paid those sums, rightfully or wrongfully I do not know, hut I suppose rightly as usual.

It is not treating parliament or the country fairly to lead us to suppose that $3,000 is the entire contribution of tlie country to the living expenses of Mr. Justice Dugas or any other judge, and I am. coming to some of the other judges. Why were these items of heat and lighting paid besides the $3,000 ?

I have no other explanation than the one I have given. It was the policy of the past, and Judge Dugas has complained over and over again that he could not live on his salary, in spite of all we have been paying him. I quite grant that it seems extraordinary that we should have to pay for the lighting and so on.
What does the item in the Auditor General's Report on page V-49, for court house aud judge's quarters, Dawson, $430, mean ?
That means the court house and the judge's room there.
Under the heading of Judge Dugas' residence, I do not observe any rental. How is his rental provided ?
We are paying $150 a month for his reutal also.
Where does that appear in the Auditor General's Report ?
I have got it down in my notes that we are paying that.

I have only such information as is found in the Auditor General's Report. On page V-19, I find under- the heading of 'Judge Craig's residence, Dawson,' that we paid the Alaska Commercial Company for a stove $25; the Dawson Electric Light & Power Company $49.50 for installing lights, and $191 for lighting; and that we paid D. A. Matheson for firewood, $759, and the North-west Mounted Police for firewood $8G.G3. We paid also to the Yukon Saw Mill Company for 4 book cases $70. Did Mr. Justice Craig have the residence and did the country pay for it ?

The position is as I have described it. We have simply paid in the past for the judge's residence and lighting and fuel. I am not in a position to explain every item in the Auditor General's Report. The Public Accounts Committee would be the better place to have those explanations.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Can the hon. minister give us the items composing $48,000 he is asking in this vote ? If some of these go into next year, we will have to strike off the amount in next year's estimates.
These are obligations that we have to pay to the 1st of July this year, and that will be all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If Judge Dugas and Judge Craig went out there on a salary of $5,000 and $3,000 living allowance, who is it that has violated the law by paying them more? It must be either the Department of Public Works or the Department of Justice. These items were paid at Dawson and the vouchers sent here, and the Auditor General passed the voucher. The accounts did not pass through the Auditor General's hands before payment at all.
The hon. gentleman will not ask me to repudiate our obligations. We have rented those houses and must pay for them till the 1st of July.
