speechtext:
Then you can deduct what you have overpaid from the judges salaries to the 1st of July. Each judge is entitled to $5,000 salary and $3,000 living Hon. Mr. TARTE.
expenses and to nothing more, and if the country has paid anything more, he ought to be made to refund it. Each went out there under a stipulated bargain of $5,000 a year salary, and $3,000 a, year expenses. And he could live there for $1,000 a year if he wanted to. This $3,000 living expenses was to cover house rent, fuel, light, &e. Why does the Minister of Public Works. come to the rescue of this judge and say : We will pay you $4,000 more in the form of house rent, lighting, cord wood and so on 1 Somebody has authorized it or it would not have been paid. Either the Minister of Justice's department is responsible, or else the Minister of Public Works' department has done it of its own accord. But it is contrary to law, and surely the hon. minister does not want to force through the House a vote that is contrary to law. We do not want to repudiate a just debt. But here is debt that we did not fairly incur. If it is paid, it should be taken from the judge's salary.

Here is a case in which the Minister of Justice should exercise the power of his office. The hon. minister states on the floor of this House that Judge Dugas was appointed with an allowance of $3,000 for living expenses. The Minister of Public Works asks us how it tomes that the Auditor General would pass this item of house rent if it was not right. It was because the $3,000 living expenses was put in that way so that the Auditor General could not question it. The Minister of Public Works states that this was in addition to living allowance expenses. But the Minister of Justice tells us that this $3,000 living allowance was to include the rent. That being so, the Minister of Justice should see to it that Judge Dugas is brought to some settlement, or he is not fit to occupy the position of Minister of Justice.

The Minister of Justice can only say that, so far as any expenditures in the past are concerned he will be glad to inquire into them, and when he has informed himself will be ready to come back here and talk about the matter. I can only tell what the judges were entitled to receive. And I will be responsible, for the future, to see that this $5,000 is given as a living allowance, and that the judges shall not get rent, fuel, light, and so on in addition. I will undertake that.
But is it not the hon. minister's duty to see that the wrong of the past is righted ?

It is my fluty to ascertain the facts, and, having ascertained the facts, to consider what I will do. But my hon. friend surely will not ask me to take as facts all the statements made here to-night. They are made, of

course, in good faith, and to the best of belief of those who make them.
But I am taking the hon. minister's statement that Judge Dugas was appointed with a living allowance of $3,000, which was to include these items.
I have not withdrawn any statement which I made.

If the minister has . made the statement that this living allowance was iutended to include these items, and if, as a matter of fact, these items have been paid over and above the living allowance, is it not his duty as Minister of Justice to see that this money is refunded ? And will he not do that, so that, next session, when he comes before the House, he will be able to tell us that the money has been refunded?
Next session I shall be glad to answer any questions that shall be put to me. But I am not going to say now what I will do next session.
But will not the hon. gentleman say now what he will do about an expenditure that was made wrongfully-I do not say wilfully so, but perhaps through some clerical mistake ?

There has been no clerical mistake. I have been told by the late Minister of Justice that I was bound to pay for rental, fuel and light. Right or wrong, that is the way I was instructed.
Mr: REID (Grenville). That is a fair statement'on the part of the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and exonerates him from responsibility. But. it makes clearer the duty of the Minister of Justice to see that this wrong is righted. I ask the Minister of Justice if he will see to it that this is made right.
The appeal to do what is right is heard, and will be dealt with accordingly.

The Minister of Justice must recollect that this does not in the slightest degree depend on statements made by my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard). We are depending upon the public records in the report of the Auditor General. If the living allowance of $3,000 excludes these items of rent and so on, the Minister of Justice can come next year and say that the increase of $5,000 also excludes them. Or if my hon. friend should not happen to be Minister of Justice when these items are discussed next year, the hon. gentleman who occupies the position at that time might do the same as, apparently, the late Minister of Justice-if we are to accept literally the statement of the Minister of Public Works-has done. I do think,
5. 1902	4206
with all respect, that it will be necessary for the Minister of Justice to investigate this matter. I do not understand him to say that he will not investigate. On the contrary, I understand that he will. And it requires a thorough investigation. Because, of course, apart from anything the Minister of Justice may say, we know that a living allowance should include rental and a number of other items that have been charged. These things are not to be dealt with according to the opinion of the Minister of Justice for the time being as to what is right or what is wrong, but according to the law and to the vote of parliament. The vote (Of parliament was for a living allowance, and outside of that, these gentlemen have no more right to have their houses furnished than any judge in Ontario or Nova Scotia. Would the hon. Minister of Justice say that, outside of this living allowance, a judge in the Yukon had a right to have his house furnished, to have electric light provided or to have carpenter work done at the public*, expense any more than a judge in any other part of the Dominion of Canada? I cannot understand on what principle he would be entitled to it. And I do not think the Minister of Justice can suggest any.
I have not tried to suggest any.
I quite understand that.

My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will understand the position I take. By statute the judge is entitled to receive a salary of $5,000. In addition, $3,000 yearly is placed in the estimates as a living allowance. I understood that this $3,000 was paid to these gentlemen for the purpose of placing them relatively in the same position as if they were living in one of the older provinces, an allowance being necessary on account of the increased cost of living in the Yukon. Now, I cannot deal with understandings and policies with respect to expenditures; I can only deal with facts, with the statutes and the estimates. I find that the statute provides a salary of $5,000 and the estimates contain a living allowance of $3,000. That is all I know. Next year this difficulty cannot occur, so far as I am concerned. Because when the question arose about increasing the living allowance to the judges of the Yukon, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition asked me to explain. If the hon. gentleman will refer to the ' Hansard ' report of what I said, he will find that I took up the list of expenses, and said that the allowance was to be increased because of the amount of expenditure that is necessary to put a judge in the Yukon in the same relative position as one in the older provinces. Going over the list, I found the first item was $150 a month for house rent,

420S

then so much for light, so much for fuel, and so much for servants' wages. I think I even gave the price of bread and beef and other things out there. In view of that, if anything was paid to these gentlemen in addition, I do not know how I could explain it to the House-it would be impossible for me to do so. Of course, I have no control over any expenditure except that of the money placed in my charge. In this case, there is a salary and a living allowance, which is fixed at $5,000. Beyond that, my authority does not go. If my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works states in his place that he was requested to provide these gentlemen with residences and, in addition, to supply them with furniture for these residences, and further to supply light and fuel, and so on, that is a matter with which I have had nothing to do, though, of course, I accept the responsibility for what was done by my predecessor. But all I can say is that no such thing as that can occur in the future. I cannot permit it, and in view of the debate which has taken place tonight, the Minister of Public Works will not permit it either. I may say that when the matter came before council for consideration, the justification for the increase to $5,000 for living allowance was that these gentlemen should receive it directly and not indirectly, outside of their salary.

Let me say that not only have I been asked to pay for the rent, but that the Department of Justice has written me a dozen letters at least asking me to build residences for the judges. Not very long ago I received requisitions to build residences for those judges, and in the meantime, pending their erection, I have been requested to pay the rents, and for lighting and fuel. The Department of Justice has over and over again urged upon me the erection of residences for those two judges. Whether my hon. friend will do it in future is for him to say.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I presume the Minister of Public Works has authority from the late Minister of Justice authorizing the payment of these amounts. If he will bring that down it will relieve the minister.

I do not say that I have the written authority for everything that the government has decided to do, that is not the way business is done. But I say I have many letters asking me to erect residences for the two judges there, and in the meantime it has been decided to pay for rent, fuel and lighting.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Surely the Minister of Justice would not violate the law without authority.
I do not know that I have violated the law.

The Minister of Public Works of course relieves himself of the responsibility by reason of the Justice Department giving him the instructions; and the Minister of Justice relieves himself from responsibility by saying that it was done by his predecessor. However, I think that the Minister of Public Works is entitled to a little share of this responsibility.
I take it all.

Perhaps now we can find out exactly whether in this $3,000 the rental was included. We have the Minister of Finance here who will perhaps explain it, because when Judge Dugas was appointed to the Yukon this $3,000 living expenses was of course brought up in the council. Was there not a statement showing how these living expenses were made up, and whether the rental was included in that $3,000 ?

I am afraid I can hardly undertake to tell the hon. gentleman how every item approved by the council was made up. In regard to the Yukon affairs, we recognized there were conditions out there which differed from those in old Canada, and allowances were made upon a liberal scale regarding the officers in a way that would not be done in the older portions of the Dominion. As this regards the departments of the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Public Works, I would hesitate to express an opinion about it, but I do not hesitate to say, from the discussion that lias taken place here to-night, it is quite evident that Judge Dugas received a sum of money which the present Minister of Justice did not suppose he would have received under the arrangement. Before the Minister of Justice takes any action in that matter, it is only right he should endeavour to find out the circumstances under which this order was given. But we do not divide responsibility. The government as a whole must accept the responsibility. Whatever may be said as to the liberality of this allowance in the past, the present Minister of Justice has declared that there shall not be any such allowance in the future. I agree entirely with the hon. gentlemen opposite that the payment of the allowances in this loose way is entirely objectionable. We should give a reasonable, even a liberal sum for living allowance in that country, but that should include everything of the kind, and there should not be a penny expended in the manner of these charges that appear in the Auditor General's account. I am inclined to think as respects the past that the judge has been receiving a more liberal allowance probably than he should.
I think the case might be put more forcibly even than the Minister of Justice or the Minister of

Finance has put. I was trying to discover the vote out of which-this has been paid, it has been paid apparently out of the Yukon public buildings. It would be just as right for the Minister of Public Works to pay the rent for the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Justice out of the vote for Dominion public buildings generally for Ontario, as for these expenditures to have been paid out of the votes from which they have been paid. I do not see the least distinction between the two. It would be just as wrong, just as unjustifiable, for the Minister of Public Works to have paid the house rent for himself or the Minister of Finance as to pay for this house rent out of this vote, whether he did that by direction of the Minister of Justice or of any one else. I would hesitate to suppose that the late Minister of Justice would have ordered these expenditures to have been paid out of a vote of that kind. It seems to me that this question demands the very closest investigation on the part of the Minister of Justice and on the part of the Minister of Finance, who is the guardian of the treasury. I appreciate the fact that they cannot give a full explanation at the moment, or say what course will be pursued without looking into the question. I think it well that the matter has been brought to their attention to-night, and I trust the investigation which they make will be thorough and complete, and one that will enable them to come down to the House with a satisfactory statement with regard to these matters at some later date.

There is a still more objectionable feature in regard to this vote. Here is a vote of $3,000 for living allowance and $5,000 salary, $8,000 altogether. Surely the Auditor General is aware whether the rental should be included in this $3,000. How did it pass the Auditor General's Department ? That is the extraordinary part of it. Perhaps the vote was set free for public buildings in the Yukon territory, and the money was taken out of that. The Auditor General is responsible to this House, and he is under the direction of the Minister of Finance. There is no justification for his course whatever. What is the use of our voting particular items for particular purposes if they can be applied to other purposes. The Auditor General is the guardian of these votes to see that they are properly applied. He does not seem to have done so in this respect.

Will not the hon. gentleman admit that the word ' rents ' cover these things ? We had a vote last year under the head of ' rents ' for public buildings in the Yukon. The policy of the Department of Justice from 'the very beginning was to erect residences for the judges, and until they were erected we have been paying rents.

I do not think it would be fair that we should take refuge behind the Auditor General in this matter. My impression is that this money was paid out of a letter of credit, and the Auditor General probably was not aware of it until after the payment was made. If so, the most that can be said of it is that the Auditor General when he had the accounts submitted to him should have drawn attention to the matter.

That is the fact. There was a credit given to the department for a certain sum of money, and out of that sum this expenditure has been made. Then it was the duty of the Auditor General when he found an expenditure which was not justified by vote of parliament to draw attention of parliament to it. He should have said that here was an expenditure over and above the amount that was voted by parliament for that particular purpose.

Mr. KAULBACH, Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has given any recognition to the appeals which I have made in regard to the breakwater at Petit Riviere and also the breakwater at Mill Cove in St. Margaret's Bay in the county of Lunenburg, and also the retaining wall at Battery Point at the mouth of Lunenburg Harbour. I would like to call the attention of the hon. minister to the work at Skinner's Pond. An expenditure of about $2,000 was made two years ago for this work. Nothing has been done there since. This is a very necessary work and I may say that there was a channel opened through the sand from the pond to the gulf. That channel was closed up last fall. At the time of the opening of the channel a dam was built across the old outlet from the pond and this was closed up. When the sea had closed the new channel the pond overflowed its banks, there being no outlet from the pond, and the consequence was, that the farmers found that the ground up to their doors was flooded with water. They petitioned the hon. Minister of Public Works that some action should be taken last fall. I forwarded that petition myself, and I would ask, inasmuch as this expenditure of about $2,000 was made two years ago, that he followed it up by a further expenditure to assist the farmers and fishermen living on that part of the coast where they are very much in want of this accommodation. It is very much required. There is no harbour from Tignish to Miminegasli, a distance of 30 miles along the coast. These people are obliged to use small fishing boats, whereas if they had Skinner's Pond harbour kept open sufficiently to admit a larger sized craft, they could pursue their industry with greater success and perhaps the hon. gentleman will see whether we can get an amount placed in the supplementary estimates next year for this purpose.

I do not remember that our resident engineer has called attention to that work. I thought it was completed. I was under the impression that all the work, necessary there had been done. The chief engineer will take' note of it, but at the same time Mr. I-Iegan has not called our attention to the necessity of any further work there.

That may be, but the people petitioned last fall. I am aware that the hon. minister received the petition because he replied to my letter forwarding the petition. That should be sufficient notice. He said that he would consult Mr. Hegan, the engineer about the work.. It is no fault of the people who have been urging upon the department the necessity for this work. Will the minister say that it will be provided for in the supplementary estimates ?

I cannot say that because the supplementary estimates are closed.
Repairs, maritime provinces generally, $8,000. The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
I move that that Item be struck out.
Hear, hear.
Cannot the minister apply that amount to Skinner's Pond.
I wish to call the atten-ion of the minister to the works at Oro-mocto on the St. John river. What amount will likely be expended there.
Two plans are prepared for the work on the Oromocto river and tenders will be asked for it in a short while.
I am very glad to hear that. Does the minister intend to prosecute the work of clearing out the shoals.
Instructions have been given for a dredge to go there and as soon as a dredge can be got the work will be completed.
Under the charge of Mr. Shewan the resident engineer.
Yes.

I wish to call the attention of the minister to the much needed work of the dredging of La Have river, Malione bay, and Lunenburg harbour. There is no work in all Canada that is more necessary than the dredging of these three places. There is a very extensive shipping fleet there, and accommodation is absolutely necessary for it. Last year the minister told me he had no dredge, but I find dredges going to other places of less importance. Why cannot this work be attended to during the coming season. It was promised last year and promised the year before. There was a sum in connection with this work placed in the estimates just previous to the last election, but it was not expended. Will the minister promise me that he will send a dredge there this year. This work is in the public interest and there is nothing at all political about it. I would strongly urge this work on the attention of the minister.
My hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade)-
From Lunenburg.

No, from Annapolis, called my attention a week or two ago to this matter and because of the great importance of La Have river I fully realized that something has to be done. It is a very fine river. I was there two or three years ago and representations were made to me, but there was then no dredge available and there is not to-day. I have tried at the request of my hon. friend (Mr. Wade) and other friends to relieve the situation by ordering some rudimentary work to remove a sand bar that was formed by the flood this spring and we are trying to remove it now.

This interest shown on the part of the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) is very commendable no doubt, but the minister might have referred to the hon. member for Lunenburg as having appealed repeatedly year after year for this work. If that fact were shown and credited me it would have looked a little better and more commendable on the part of the Minister of Public Works.

I think I will have to intervene. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) could not very well have called attention last year to a sand bar which was created by the flood this year, although I have no doubt that my hon. friend (Mr. Kaulbach) would have been quite ready to call attention to it this year. There is dredging urgently needed on the La Have river,, Lunenburg harbour, and Mahone bay, and I must do my hon. friend (Mr. Kaulbach) the justice to say that he has repeatedly brought it to the attention of the House. There was a special obstruction caused this year in La Have river apart from the necessary 'dredging. It was that which my hon. friend from Annapolis brought to the notice of the Minister of Public Works. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) was for many years a resident on the La Have river, and knows it perhaps better than any man in the House. Accordingly the Minister of Public Works took steps to do the little work connected with the removal of that sand bar. There is great difficulty in finding dredges. I told my hon. friend (Mr. Kaulbach) a year ago that I would recommend the La Have river to be dredged almost before any work I was prepared to advocate in Nova Scotia. 3ut the trouble is that the smaller class of dredges which suit in other places are not adapted to the La Have river, and so far the Minister of Public Works was unable to carry out his intention of having dredging done there. He is now having a large dredge built which will be suitable for work on the La Have river, and with the assistance of that dredge that work can be done. In the case of Lunenburg, for the last year or two, there have not been urgent works except dredging.

My hon. friend has urged us repeatedly to send dredges there, and I have been as anxious as himself to see them sent; but we really have not had the dredges to do the work.

It is very kind of the minister to refer to me in the way he has done, and I appreciate it; but my reason for referring to the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. AVade) was that the hon. minister drew out the hon. member for Annapolis to speak of dredging in the county which I have the honour to represent.
I have referred in so many kind words to the efforts of my hon. friend from Lunenburg that I thought for once my hon. friend from Annapolis might have a little credit.

If you will allow me a word, I may say that I have received communications from people who are interested in having the dredging done on the La Have river and in the removal of the bar which has been referred to by the Minister of Finance. I am free to admit that while my hon. friend (Mr. Ivaulbach) represents the county of Lunenburg, the people on the La Have river have no confidence in his ability to secure dredging for them. He represented the county in the time of the late government for many years. The only dredging done in the county was in the harbour of Lunenburg, and there are people mean enough to say that his own property was benefited by it more than any other. It is only natural, therefore, that friends in Bridgewater should have written to me to urge the minister to do this work. On the very evening that I received the letter, I brought the matter to the notice of the minister, and the statement he made, I think was very satisfactory. ,

If the hon. member for Annapolis got a letter of that kind, I think that he' should in courtesy have handed it to me, and left me to make the appeal ; and then he might have supported me. That would have been kindness on his part, and what I might reasonably have expected from him. With reference to the dredging in Luneftburg harbour, the hon. gentleman knows right well that no part of it benefited me in any way, and I am sorry that he should have referred to it as he did. On the contrary,
I objected to the dredging being done where he refers to, because I wanted the harbour deepened for the purpose of improving it as a harbour of refuge for the fishermen ; and the dredging where it was done was endangering the bank of my property, as was well known to the public.

If I might be allowed to explain, this channel is near the entrance of the canal down towards the port Of Valley-field. This channel has been used a great many years and is now being used by coal barges, and barges laden with grain and lumber. In low water in the summer season there is only about 6 feet of water, and in consequence these barges are not able to load and unload to advantage. This is a very important work, and I am only sorry that a larger amount is not voted for it. When I state that the largest industry in

Valleyfield now gets 20,000 tons of coal a year, and that many barges laden with grain and lumber come into the harbour, you can well realize the importance of deepening the channel to a sufficient depth. I see that the government are spending a great deal of money for the construction of wharfs in all the older provinces. I would ask the minister if it is his intention to extend the same principle to the province of British Columbia, where we have large fishing interests, and where up to the present the government have not spent any money for wharfs ?

Senator Templeman called my attention to the Importance of British Columbia and its claims to have wharfs built in that province, and when the supplementary estimates come down, I shall probably be criticised for having provided too large a sum for this purpose.

These estimates are only for the current year. When the supplementary estimates come down, my hon. friend will have to judge whether we have acted as he wishes us to do. Until then my lips are sealed.

I would like to call the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that a wharf is badly required there, and
that the wharf which was there has been destroyed owing to its having been used by the government contractors.
My engineer tells me that we have had an examination and a survey made there lately.

I understand that.
St. Maurice district-accommodation at Grand Mere for storing and soiling logs, &c., Governor General's warrant, $63,000.
Does the government sort the logs ?

My personal opinion is that the establishment of hatcheries has proved satisfactory in other countries and also in Canada. If we find that the results have been as good as we expect I shall ask parliament for a grant for the coming year to establish more hatcheries. Of course that must depend to some extent on the information given by the experts as to the proper locality to establish a hatchery. speechtext:
There is a matter which I wished to mention to the minister in connection with the lighthouse and coast service. It is the necessity of having a lightship for the Halifax harbour.
I brought this matter to the attention of the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries two or three sessions ago-in fact, I think on two or three different occasions. Since then a statement has been placed in my hands on the matter, and, as it will take only a few moments to read it, I will take the liberty of reading it to the minister now. It is prepared by a gentleman who is intimately acquainted with the necessities of the harbour. I think there was a lightship at the mouth of the harbour a good many years ago; and, in the opinion of this gentleman and others who are familiar with the subject, the reason that lightship drifted and failed to be of service, and had to be abandoned, was that it was not properly moored. The statement which has been given me is these words :
A lightship is wanted off Halifax harbour because the existing lights and fog signals are all inside of the dangers to be avoided instead of outside. The dangers to be avoided are the Sambro ledge on the west and Thrum Cap shoal on the east. The latter Is well inside the bay formed by Chebueto Head on the west and Devil island on the east, but the former runs a long way out, nearly two miles beyond Sambro island.
In clear weather, i.e., not foggy, the lighthouses on Devil's Island, Sambro Island and Chebueto Head are sufficient guides to' the entrance, though even then it is worth noting that the [DOT] Daniel Steinmann ' was lost with 100 lives through mistaking the light on Sambro for that on Chebueto-the explanation given at the time being that the rain squalls blowing across the fixed light on Sambro caused the captain to mistake It for the revolving light on Chebueto. He ran in for it expecting to pick up a pilot, only to find himself among the maze of reef outside of Sambro island.
But in foggy weather the lights are useless, and the guides to the entrance are two automatic buoys, one to the south-east of Sambro and one further to the eastward, and fog bombs on Sambro island. An automatic buoy is a very imperfect guide. Unless there is considerable sea on it makes very little noise. Even when it is making a good deal, it is universal experience that it is quite uncertain whether you will hear it or not. It is not a loud noise and easily drowned by the noise on board a steamer. The sound often seems to act in a peculiar way, so as to be inaudible half a mile away, and yet perfectly plain several miles off. In a strong breeze it can seldom be heard any distance to windward of the buoy. In every way it is a poor mark to run for in the fog and if you do not hit it the penalty may be to find yourself among the ledges, just as the ' Portia ' did. The bombs on Sambro island are said to be very bard to locate and misleading, and they, too, are of course inside the danger. A few years ago the ship [DOT] John Maeleod,' with a cargo of sugar wandered about for two or three days in the fog looking for something to show her a course to the harbour, but found none, and eventually was lost on the Sambro ledge.
Tliis is the remedy he proposes
What is wanted is a lightship with a powerful fog horn moored well clear of the outer Sambro reefs. Such a mark could he run for in any weather day or night with perfect ease and confidence. Pilots could be kept on board.
There should be no difficulty in mooring such a vessel. The bottom is mostly sand and gravel, good holding ground. The experiment formerly tried of a lightship was bound to fail, because they tried to make the ship ride to her own anchors and two enormous chain cables, the weight of which was certain to drag her under in a seaway. What is wanted is to take weight of the cable by a large mooring and fasten the ship to the mooring. In that case a properly designed vessel would ride easily in any weather. The lightships in Great Britain and the States are mostly moored this way, I believe. Even if she could not or any accident happened, she could slip the mooring line and run up the harbour, without losing anything.

I will mention that in confidence to the hon. minister. The writer is a gentleman who has taken a good deal of interest in the subject, and the hon. minister can inquire as to whether the suggestions he made are valuable or not. I know nothing about the subject myself, but take a little interest in it on account of having brought the matter to the attention of the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries on several occasions. I asked this gentleman, who locally takes a great deal of interest in the subject, and is personally interested in the safety of the harbour, to give me a statement of his views in writing. He wrote this rather hurriedly, supposing no doubt that I would not read it to the House, but I thought it better to give his own language than attempt to sum up his remarks by any language of my own.



I trust that the hou. minister will consider the matter because there is a strong feeling among masters of vessels that something of the kind should be done, and it is quite easy to make the harbour perfectly safe by night and by day. The only subject for consideration by the minister is the best way to do this, and this gentleman thinks it can be done by a lightship, and that there would be no difficulty In doing this with the improved modern methods of constructing and placing lightships.

I had the great pleasure of visiting Halifax a short time ago, and was told that it was a magnificent harbour with a wide channel and that it had never suf- j fered from fog or ice all the year round, so that I am rather surprised to hear of any application for any improvements in connection with that harbour. However, 1 suppose that this is a little outside the harbour, and I may say that the matter was brought up some time ago and an investigation and report made. The opinion come to was that there was no such pressing necessity for this lightship, which the informant of my hou. friend seems to think there is. However, we have always to recognize that nowadays, when vessels are so much larger and swifter than formerly, aids to navigation are required that were not thought necessary some years ago. If the hon. gentleman would be kind enough to give me the memo, he has just read, I will look into the matter and give some information concerning it, when the estimates for next year come down, and I would also promise him that it will have most careful consideration by the department at an early date.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I do not think that any person in Halifax would make the statement that we do not have occasionally a little fog along the coast, though, so far as the harbour itself is concerned, I do not think that any improvement is required, as the harbour is as open and clean and safe as any harbour in the world. But what my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is referring to is not the harbour but the coast before you reach it, some miles outside, and it must be understood that we are not making any reflections on the harbour when we speak of the coast outside. We have a little fog on the coast occasionally, but nothing compared with the Bay of Fundy and over at St. John. The harbour of Halifax is as perfect as it can be, but there is no harbour in the world where there is not a little fog outside. If it were so perfect, as to be free from fog along the coast, we would not require lighthouses or anything of the kind, but in common with all harbours some little protection is required there as elsewhere.

speechtext:
Persons who are at all acquainted with the circumstances in connection with this case will consider the vote a most extraordinary one. This is a most unsatisfactory matter to discuss in the House, because the minister who is in charge of the department had nothing to do with it, and those who are to blame, if there are any to blame, are not here to meet the charges. To hon. gentlemen who were in this House ten or twelve years ago, this claim of Noble Brothers is quite an old friend. This firm were engaged in business of fishing on Georgian Bay. I know very little personally of their operations, but I shall read from * Hansard ' the opinion of a gentleman in this House showing that they were not by any means persons deserving of much consideration. In a discussion on this same claim the bon. member who represents the adjoining riding to that in which Noble Brothers live, spoke of them in the following terms. I quote from page 2014 of 'Hansard' of 1895:
I know that I have been spoken to dozens of times by fishermen with regard to the reputation of the Nobles, and I merely give this as a justification for the seeming harsh course which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries adopted in this case. When I have been endeavouring to get these men off time after time, it has been said to me :	Why take the Nobles part, they
are perfect outlaws ; they fish with nets that are larger than the law allows ; they fish out of season, they violate the law in every way. They say : You cannot prosecute them because they are so strong and have such powerful influence at their backs, the department is afraid to prosecute them, but they pile unto us because we are individually alone, and we cannot bring that force to bear against the department which they can.
These remarks were made by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), who, I regret to see, is not in his place, but who, if he were here, I am sure, would join with me in protesting against this vote. These remarks were made when the present Hon. Senator Danderkin, then the representative of South Grey in this House endeavoured to bring the same case under the review of parliament. Let me now refer to some of the circumstances of this claim. These Noble Brothers, who -were engaged, as 1

say, in fishing, year in and year out, season in and season out, had openly and in the most flagrant way defied the laws of the land in connection with the fisheries. This is shown by the evidence in the case laid on the Table of the House by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. That evidence shows that they supplied seine nets, trap nets and other illegal fishing gear to halfbreeds and Indians, and in return, took a share of the fish caught by these illegal means. After they had been trespassers against the laws for years, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of that time, Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper, determined to bring them to time. They were notified that, in consequence of the flagrant outrages they had perpetrated in the past, evidence of which was before the department, they would not be granted licenses. Having a large fishing plant, consisting of tugs, fishing smacks and a large quantity of nets, they came down here in 1893 after having received notice that no consideration would be allowed them for the future. They proffered their money to the license inspector, Mr. Elliott, but finding that a license would not be issued, one of the firm came down to Ottawa. The hon. member for East Grey, knowing Mr. Noble, accompanied him to the minister and endeavoured to intervene on his behalf. And the hon. member for East Grey gives this account of the interview:
Mr, Noble admitted himself in the presence of the minister that he knew of the change in the regulations the fall before. He admitted also that after he paid his money, that he was told before his boats went out that he was not likely to get his license. When that Information came *to his knowledge he came down to Ottawa to Intercede with the department in hopes he might induce them to give him his license, and on the very day ho was here, and when we were pleading on his behalf In the office, a telegram came from the fishery overseer saying that his boats were out fishing in the Georgian Bay.
Let bon. members get tbe full meaning of these facts. Here were two partners who bad been officially advised that tbe department would refuse them a license. One of the partners comes to Ottawa to see the minister, and while he is actually laying his case before the minister, tbe inspector advises the department that, in open violation of tbe law, a license not having been issued to them, this firm were out on tbe lakes with their plant. I do not intend to speak personally of tbe operations of these men, because X do not know tbe facts. I can only say that, if general repute about Georgian Bay, where their operations are carried on, goes for anything, not a word that was said by the hon. member for East Grey concerning these people is too hard or too strong or too severe. The inspector, in pursuance of his instructions seized the tug and fishing plant of these men, and, it was tied up-there is no doubt about that- for a whole season. They had openly violat-
133J
ed the law, and the minister was quite justified, as the House at that time believed, in acting as he did. And what next happened ? These gentlemen employed solicitors to prosecute a claim against the department. The minister granted them a hearing before Judge Johnson-I believe it was-as commissioner. The evidence was thoroughly gone into. When the case came before the department, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of that time, Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper, told these people point blank that they could have a fiat at any time to go into the courts if they thought their claim against the government was a good one. As often as this fiat was offered to these wrongdoers-for they were wrongdoers-so often was it declined. After a time Sir Charles Hibert Tupper left the department, but the gentleman who succeeded him also declined to allow the claim. Meantime, some very powerful friends of the Conservative government, relatives of these Noble Brothers used every occasion to put the pistol to the bead of the department to compel it to yield. But Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper refused to recede an inch, but told them they could rest upon their rights, a fiat would be given and they could go into tbe courts. But, knowing the ground upon which they stood, these people, very properly, from their point of view, refused to go into courts. When the change of government came in 1896, the matter stood as it had stood for three or four years before.
But, no sooner was there a change of government than the Noble Bros., being prominent supporters of the hon. gentlemen opposite, exerted their own political leverage ; and, knowing one of these gentlemen personally as I do, I saw him here session in and session out, and it was notorious what his business was. He was endeavouring to have the government take up this alleged claim and deal with it on its merits. I am glad to say for the credit of the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Sir Louis Davies, that from 1896 that gentleman resisted the payment of this claim. 1 do not know whether he offered them a fiat to go into the courts, I assume probably he did ; had he followed the action of his predecessor in office he certainly would have done that. But there is one thing certain, and that is that Sir Louis Davies nevejr agreed-because there was never any vote in the estimates for such a purpose-to compromise with these people in any shape or manner, so far at least as the records of the House showed by a vote of money. There was the action, first, of Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper offering them a fiat for them to go into court, and their refusal to do so. Then here is the palpable fact that for five years Sir Louis Davies would not recede from the position of the former minister and would not pay these people one dollar ; at least the evidence that is open and above board as to no

money grant being voted in the House would show conclusively that he agreed with the action of his predecessor in office, and did nothing in that regard. Now, I find on the 22nd of August, 1901, the then minister, Sir Louis Davies, appointed Mr. Justice Lount, one of the judges of the Superior Court in the province of Ontario, under a commission to inquire into this matter ; and I will be bound to say that there never was before, and I doubt if there ever will be again, a document issued from any government in this country within the terms and under the circumstances that this one was issued. Let me read for the benefit of the committee the instructions of the Order in Council to the commissioner :
By the said commission and Order in Council the following matters are submitted to me for my opinion and1 finding :-
(a)	Whether in my opinion on the facts proved before me the conviction, seizure and confiscation mentioned in the said Order in Council were justifiable or not ; and if I find such conviction, seizure and confiscation were Justifiable :
(b)	Then, whether there were any and what extenuating circumstances in connection with violations by Messrs. J. & C. Noble and their fishermen of the fishery laws and regulations, and
(c)	Whether in equity and good conscience, having regard to all the circumstances proved the government of Canada, should pay to the said Messrs. J. & C. Noble, any damages by reason of such conviction, seizure and consequent disposal of their tugs, boats, gear and nets, and the reason why in my opinion the government of Canada should pay any, and
(d)	If I fiDd that damage should be paid by the government of Canada in equity and good conscience on account of the conviction, seizure and subsequent disposal of such tugs, boats, gear and nets, what amount of damages and the reasons why in my opinion the government of Canada should pay the amount determined ; with further authority to me to recommend to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as to what disposition of all questions of costs in connection with this commission and the proceedings had and taken thereunder to me shall seem proper.
The learned judge goes on to make liis findings, and be says :-
In my opinion on the facts proved before me, the conviction, seizure and confiscation mentioned in said Order in Council were justifiable for the following reasons :
I need not read the reasons in detail which he sets out. Then he goes on to say :
Under a strict interpretation of the said S.S. 3, it was the duty of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to cause to be seized and confiscated all the materials, implements or appliances used in violation of the Act.
Further on he says :
I have therefore now to determine whether or not there were any and what extenuating circumstances on the facts proved before me which should be taken into consideration in connection with the violations by the said Nobles and their fishermen of the fishery laws and regulations, and whether in equity and good con-Mr. BENNETT.
science, having regard to all the circumstances proved, the government should pay to the said Nobles any damages hy reason of such conviction, seizure and subsequent disposal of their tugs, boats, gear and nets.
Now, it will be seen the commissioner found
that the seizure and action were justified by reason of their violations of the Act, and that all that had been done in the premises was justifiable. Then he next puts the question, hedged in by these words that the minister had inserte'd to let the Nobles fall easily, * in equity and in conscience as to what amount of damages should be paid, if any.' Now, the minister, in a case that he had refused to take up for five years, had refused to pay any damages on all the facts and evidence which was before him, because there had been a prior inquiry before Judge Johnston as commissioner, and if there was any decision to be given the then minister had all this evidence and could come to a conclusion as easily as the judge. The case was pressed strongly by the law firm with which a member of this House is connected. And here again we see that principle that is coming to the front more and more everyday in this House, and is coming to be a by word and a reproach in this House, namely, the steering of cases in every department of the government by men who are members of this House, or by their partners. Why, these hon. gentlemen made the welkin ring when they were in opposition on this very question. It was notorious that for years they denounced the action of the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy in holding a brief in the St. Catharines Milling Company, although Mr. McCarthy stated time and again that he did not participate in any of the fees that came to his office through that ease.
Well, Sir, the case apparently was put in good trim, a partner of an hon. member of this House is retained on behalf of the Nobles; and then, so as to make their fall easy with these words ' in equity and good conscience,' the learned judge goes into the disposition of the case. The minister this afternoon laid the papers on the Table containing the evidence; there are 800 or 900 pages which it is difficult to wade through. I have glanced over it, and I find that page after page of that evidence proves every allegation that could be made against these men. The counsel for the government, Mr. Lindsay, was acting, I think, with commendable vigour in resisting the claim on behalf of the department-and I have no fault to find from what I have seen of the evidence in that regard-and Mr. Lindsay was told by7 the counsel of the Noble Bros, that he need not call any more witnesses to prove that they had supplied illegal nets to half-breeds who had participated in the fish that were taken out of these nets, and the evidence was so preponderating that these men did systematically defy the law for years, that it was admitted there was no necessity for calling some eighteen of

those witnesses who were standing there in court to prove that the Noble Bros., had been supplying them with these illegal fishing nets. More than that, it was shown in evidence by their own bookkeeper when the books were produced, that year in and year out they had fish caught illegally in their storehouse for sale ; they made no bones about it, and one of their witnesses makes even this strong allegation, that as soon as the fishery inspector came there to make a seizure, one of the Nobles suggested to his assistant the propriety of ' fixing ' Mr. Elliott the fishery inspector, evidently supposing that for a monetary consideration the inspector could be fixed, and there would be no prosecution. You can find in different parts of the evidence this fact, that when the inspector came there they bundled a large quantity, one witness states over a ton, of these illegal nets, trap nets, pound nets and seine nets into boxes, and then when the inspector came to look through their storehouse, of course nothing was to be found.
Now, I have this to say, that I am going to enter my protest, although it will not have any weight with the committee, I assume, and as far as the whole case is to be discussed it is most unsatisfactory because the hon. gentleman who is now at the head of the department had nothing to do with it beyond simply finding it when he came into office. I may say that throughout the country and particularly on the shores of Georgian Bay it will be a most startling thing when it is known that these Noble Brothers are to get $18,563 for systematically breaking the law, for telling the Fisheries Department that they did not care what power or influence they had, that they were prepared to bring influence to bear. When the Conservative party were in power they were being buttressed up by strong Conservative friends and when the change of government came I know not what they have done since then. In view of the strong language I have read from [DOT] Hansard,' uttered by the hon. member for East Grey, I would be bound to say that the statements made by him on that occasion will be amply borne out. Here was this officer of the law doing his duty fearlessly, as I know. More than once when 1 was a supporter of the old government in parliament from 1891 to 1896, I had time and again to appeal to Sir Hifobert Tupper for what ? Because, the men doing exactly what these men were doing, fishing with illegal nets, had their nets and boats seized, and it was proper that they should be seized. If a man wanted to take the chance there was the law set for him, and if he was found fishing illegally he had to suffer the consequences. I can recall instance after instance where fishermen who had their all invested in an equipment consisting of boats and nets, had the mortification of seeing their property burned up on the shore right under their very eyes in an endeavour to stop this illegal fishing. These men can now look back knowing what they had to suffer by reason of having contravened the law. While these Noble Brothers who were the greatest poachers and the greatest wrongdoers, the men who had been spoiling the whole fishing business on the lakes, are to be rewarded by the government with this princely grant of $18,563, of which I believe some $3,000 is to go as law costs to a firm of which a member of this House is a partner. I can only say that I enter my protest against voting this money.

I fear we will find a great deal of difficulty in enforcing the fishery regulations. I have a statement furnished me by the department in regard to this matter, and I will place it before the committee :
In 1894, the fishing tugs, boats and gear of the Messrs. J. & C. Noble, of Killarney, were seized by the fishery overseer for the district under instructions from the department, for having been used for fishing purposes without having first obtained a license therefor as required by law, and the Messrs. Noble were, during the year, refused licenses and their tugs, boats and gear confiscated. These were eventually returned in bond in time for the fishing season of 1895.
Even during the time of the previous government, there was quite a difference of opinion as to the punishment which should be inflicted upon these people for the violation of the law that had occurred. After having these tugs, gear and boats under seizure for a long time, they were eventually returned :
Meanwhile strong representations were made that the offence committed was mrely a technical one under the circumstances, and that the punishment received by the Nobles was far in excess of that demanded by the irregularity committed by them.
Thie correspondence continued from 1894 to the fall of 1901, during which time two commissions were granted to inquire into the claim of the Messrs. Noble for damages, neither of which ever reached a conclusion, the counsel for the Messrs. Noble being unable to accept the terms of reference to the commissioners, and the commissioners' ruling on strictly legal grounds.
In 1901 the government consented to refer the matter for a final decision to a commissioner in the person of the Hon. Justice Lount, one of the Judges of the High Court of Justice of the province of Ontario, and in the terms of reference to the commissioner the element of good conscience and equity was admitted, as well as that of strict law.
I may say to my hon. friend and to the committee that we all remember that there was a great difference of opinion in regard to this question. It is true that the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Char-

les Hibbert Tupper) took a very extreme view, but bis successor, tbe Hon. Mr. Cos-tigan, took a different view to a very considerable extent, and the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies) did not see his way clear
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. minister whether the return of the property was made while Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper was minister, or while Hon. Mr. Cos-tigan was minister ? I am not sure myself.

I would not like to be certain about that, but it was under the administration of either one or other of these ministers and during the time of the former government. Sir Louis Davies did not see his way clear to granting any redress except in the way of a further departmental investigation, which did not seem at all satisfactory. My hon. friend has laid some stress upon the government of the day in granting this commission, but I may say that I think all governments as well as parliament are susceptible to public opinion, and I believe there was a strong opinion not only in the locality, but throughout many portions of the province of Ontario, that these people had been harshly treated. One of the brothers, it is known, died in poverty as a result of this punishment, and there was a strong public opinion that the matter should be referred for judicial action. Sir Louis Davies resisted the applications that were made from time to time, and although I was not a member of the government at that time and do not remember the exact circumstances, I have no doubt that he gave way to public opinion and granted a hearing in this matter. The result was a finding by the commissioner awarding the Messrs. Noble as damages, sustained under the circumstances proved before him, the sum of $15,563, with a further sum for legal and other expenses in connection with the last commission of $3,-
000.	I looked into this matter a few days ago and I wish to say that this is a very small portion of the cost to which these people have been put during all these years while the matter was in dispute. The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) referred to the counsel in this case being a partner of an hon. member of this House. Perhaps that is hardly fair, because, I understand that from 1894 onward and during the whole progress of this case the same firm have been counsel and solicitors for the Nobles. So that, in that case it cannot be charged that there was any fav-ounitsm, or any favour shown to a member of this House, or to the firm of which he is a partner, nor has there been any political favour shown him.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The member at that time was on the Tory side.
Yes, but that was during the time of the Tory government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is now on the Grit side.

The solicitor was on the Tory side, I am sorry to say. I mention that incidentally, because a wrong impression may be taken from the remarks of the hon. member for East Simcoe. Perhaps it is not intended to suggest that any extra influence has been brought to bear by the present member who happens to be a partner in that firm. The two late lamented members of the firm perhaps would have as much if not more political influence under both governments than the younger member of the firm. However that may be, I think this commission was appointed simply on account of the strong public opinion existing, and the feeling that injustice had been done.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: In view of the decision in this matter, I presume the minister is prepared to pay every fisherman in the Dominion who had his property confiscated for illegal work. I have a large number of gentlemen whose loss was pro-portionaibly as great as the Nobles, but they never squealed and took their medicine like men, I presume the minister will pay their claims.

In view of the frequent violations of the regulations, the department has dealt fairly leniently with all parties. The department generally stands by its officers in carrying out their duties. I may say that it would cost us very little if we could compromise on the same percentage as this, with almost all the vio-laters of the Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What was the original claim ?
I think it was something over $100,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If the case was one of such extreme severity, how was it that it took five years before an inquiry was granted V

An inquiry and some mitigation had been granted under the Conservative government, and a minister does not like to reopen a question that has been decided by his predecessor. I believe it was due to the strong public opinion that existed that a judicial inquiry should be held.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
It seems to be a rather remarkable thing that a reference should have been made in these terms, when in other departments of government

it lias been impossible to get fiats granted for tlie enforcement of claims purely on legal grounds. Three years ago twenty-four claims were presented to the Postmaster General in which the people only asked a legal enforcement of their rights, but a fiat lias not yet been granted, while this claim has been referred to a special -commissioner with the proviso that he is to report not only the legal rights of the parties, but also as to whether, apart from legal considerations, they have a fair claim against the government. This commissioner has found that these gentlemen pleaded guilty to the offence; that the seizure of their boats was justified in law, but notwithstanding the minister proposes to pay them $18,000 on account of certain considerations. If that favour be granted to these men, it is remarkable that twenty-four other Canadians who have claims against the government in respect to post office contracts are not allowed to enforce their legal claims in the courts of the country, simply because some minister refuses to report favourably on the granting of a fiat. Can the Minister of Marine explain why one practice prevails in his department and a practice of so remarkably a different character prevails in the department of the Postmaster General ?

I do not think I can explain the ways of the law. The members of the legal profession are very peculiar sometimes and if the Postmaster General were present he no doubt would be able to give his reasons. However, this was a departmental matter, and it could have been dealt with by the department at the time of the offence by inflicting a much smaller penalty. Personally, I always have been willing, both in the management of public affairs and my own private affairs, that a fair bearing should be given to both sides of case, with the view of arriving at a fair settlement. Speaking for myself, and not belonging to the legal profession, unless it is a question, of policy on which the government and parliament takes a stand, I am inclined to think that I would be always in favour of referring these matters to a proper tribunal for hearing rather than have them stand before the department for a long period, resulting in costs both to the country and to the parties themselves.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
But the matters to which I have referred are just as much of a departmental character as this. The Postmaster General saw fit to_ cancel contracts entered into for the carriage of mails, and the persons whose contracts are cancelled are advised by counsel that the Postmaster General had no right to do so. They applied for a petition of right to assert their claims, but years have passed and they have not received a single word of satisfaction. The Noble Brothers were offered six years ago a fiat in the Court of
Exchequer which they did not want because they knew they could not succeed, but these other men have been vainly trying to obtain that for three years past. After having refused a fiat these gentlemen were allowed to have their- claims investigated by^ a special commissioner, not upon the question of legal liability but on grounds infinitely more favourable to them.
I have not had an opportunity of reading the report of the commissioner very fully.
I understand that the recommendation lie makes to the government is that this claim should be paid to these men, because an officer of the government acted wilfully and in bad faith, and misled the deputy minister of Marine and Fisheries at that time as to the real facts of the case, and he has no doubt that if the real facts had been communicated to the department at that time the forfeiture would not have been enforced. Well, I do not know whether or not any claim could have been made against the government in the Court of Exchequer on that ground. I should think not. I have not considered the question, but I should think that the claim, so far as there could be a legal claim, would be against the officer himself, and that the government would not be responsible for a wilfully wrong act done by this man against these people. I suppose the Crown in that case is not legally liable, even on the report of this commissioner; and it is only as a matter of grace and favour that this vote is being put before the House at the present time. But I rose merely for the purpose of contrasting the consideration granted to these men with the utter lack of consideration granted to the men of whom I have spoken, who have been for three years asking for the right to file a petition in the Exchequer Court for the purpose of obtaining only their rights, and for no favour or grace of any kind whatever.

Was there any reason why there should have been a special commissioner in this case, or why it should not have been tried in the Exchequer Court? I understand that a fiat had been offered to these gentlemen for a number of years. If they had a legal claim, I cannot see why it was not referred to the judge of the Exchequer Court, and it looks as if they were afraid to go before him, and wanted a special commissioner who might be more favourable to them. Is there any reason why it should not have gone to the Exchequer Court ?	.

So far as I have been able to form an opinion, I do not think they would have had much chance of succeeding purely on legal grounds, and I think it was a wise act on the part of the government, if the matter was to be considered at all, to refer it to a judge of the High Court to take evidence; and he has found that the

department were not in possession of all the knowledge they should have had, or perhaps their decision would have been different. I think it is rather commendable than otherwise that the matter was taken away from here and referred to a judge who was altogether independent.	[DOT]
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It is simply like kicking a dead cat to discuss the matter now, because the minister is not at all responsible for what has been done, and I suppose the government are bound by the finding of the judge. But I can only say that if the last Minister of Marine and Fisheries were standing here and trying to get this vote through, it would certainly be a matter of wonderment why this claim, if it was a fair and honest claim, was allowed to stand for five years without any action being taken in regard to it. It was not because the claim was not pressed, because the Nobles were haunting the corridors for weeks endeavouring to get this claim through.
Has the Minister of Justice considered whether the report of the commissioner discloses any legal liability on the part of the Crown?

I have not looked into the matter very fully. According to the report, the whole proceedings were the result of a conspiracy started by this man Elliott. The learned judge finds that the fishery overseer deliberately plotted to bring about the ruin of the Nobles in accordance with threats which he had previously made to outside parties, and he goes on to say :
la my opinion, if the facts as they have been made to appear before me in the sworn testimony of many of the witnesses, and in the ex-hibts filed, had been present to the mind of the minister, such severe treatment would not have been dealt out to the Nobles. The seizure would have been abandoned.
Then he goes on to say:
The said overseer Elliott acted in bad faith, with malice and with a desire to injure and destroy the business of the said Nobles. He wilfully made false and misleading reports to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
He further goes on:
I find that the evidence given before me by the said Elliott was not given with candour or truth, and I distributed it when in conflict with the evidence of reputable witnesses.
Might I ask, is that officer Elliott still .in the service of the government ?
I do not know.

Then I find it stated that they pleaded guilty, and a witness who was examined before the commissioner, a man named Long, said that they pleaded guilty on an undertaking being practically given to them by a solicitor of the government at the time, that the result of a plea of guilty would be a favourable report to the Minister of Marine at Ottawa, and that this would restore them to their former standing. It seems to me, under all the circumstances, that there was something sufiiciently peculiar in the whole ease to justify the action of the department in referring it to the commissioner.

I have not gone into the evidence fully, but it will be borne out by the report that there was one conviction got against these people. Let me ask the Minister of Justice how he reconciles these facts, that there was a sweeping condemnation of the witness Elliott by the inspector, and that there was leave and license for the solicitor of the Noble Brothers to say what be liked to this man. Time and again it appears that after the witness gave his evidence frankly and candidly-and I searched all through the evidence in vain to see where the commissioners remonstrated with him for not telling the truth- Mr. Osier charged him with having stated a series of deliberate lies. The commission did not seem to have any air or dignity about it at all events. If the commissioners had the evidence of such a gross conspiracy against the unfortunate Noble Brothers, bow is it that Sir Louis Davies could not find a tittle of proof to establish such a conspiracy in spite of all the efforts of so able a counsel as Mr. Osier. Take all the evidence before Judge Johnson and Mr. Wilmot, before whom Mr. Oslei* appeared on behalf of the Noble Brothers, and it is quite clear that Mr. Osier failed to make any proof that would justify Sir Louis Davies in concluding that there was anything savouring of conspiracy. This fact stands out strongly, that with all this evidence before him. Sir Louis Davies refrained during five years from naming auy other inquiry. In every section of the country where the Noble Brothers are known, it will be agreed that it was not a question of merit or justice, but rather a question of political pull.
To pay the estate of the late Captain W. H. Smith, R.N.R., for travelling expenses incurred by him on government business while holding the position of chairman of the Board of Examiners of Masters and Mates, and Inquiries into Wrecks, between January, 1893, and December, 1900, Captain Smith having failed to render his accounts for such expenses each year, $3,691.09.
I think he is, and I wish to state that he is just as reputable as any judge who took evidence concerning him.
I know that Captain Smith was engaged holding inquiries and was not paid his travelling expenses and I think they ought to be paid.

We made a very careful investigation. The officer of the department at Halifax. Mr. Tremaine, looked into the matter, and gave his affidavit that Captain Smith never collected his travelling expenses and that the amount was legally due.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of the Minister of Finance, House adjourned at 12.20 a.m. Tuesday.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Tuesday, May 6, 1902.
